Coagulation part I Tests

 

General methods and principles

Q. What are 3 typical methods used in coagulation testing?

●      Turbidimetric (clot based) or chronometric (aka photo-optical)

○      INR (PT), APTT, QFIB, derived Fib, TT, Protein S activity, Factor Assays

●      Chromogenic (amidolytic assays)

○      Protein C activity, AT III, alpha 2‐antiplasmin, plasminogen, heparin assay

●      Immunologic

○      ? Immunoturbidimetric: Von Willebrand Factor Antigen, D‐Dimer, IL HIT assay

 

Q. How are common clot-based assays performed - what are 3 methods of clot detection (end-point detection)?

●      Manual (tilt tube method)

●      Photo-optical

●      Electro-mechanical (fibrometer)

 

Q. What are the pros and cons of photo-optical vs mechanical methods?

 

 

Pros

Q. What is the difference between turbidimetric and nephelometric?

●      Both are dependent on light scattering

●      Turbidimetric → measure the reduction of transmitted light due to particles in the medium (fibrin formation)

●      Nephelometric → measure side-scattered light caused by particles (nephelo = nephro = your kidneys are on your sides)

 

A ± turbidimetry, B ± nephelometry

 

Q. What is the method of “manual clot detection”?

●      Manual clot detection usually is performed by a "tilt tube" method

●      "Tilt tube" method → operator pipettes the plasma and reagents into a clear test tube, starts a timer, and tilts the tube back and forth until a clot is formed

●      Clot formation is detected visually, at which point the timer is stopped.

 

Q. What is the principle and method of “photo-optical clot detection”?

 

●      Based on principle that light passing through a medium in which fibrinogen is converted to fibrin will be absorbed by fibrin strands when they form

○      Get decreased light transmission/ increase in absorbance

●      Light at 671 nm is transmitted through the plasma and monitored by a sensitive photodetector positioned 180 degrees to the incident source. Measured as OD/minute.

●      In photo optical method, detection of clot formation is measured by a change in optical density (OD) of a test sample. As the plasma sample clots, it becomes more optically dense & the amount of light falling on a photo-sensitive detector decreases (i.e. transmitted light decreases).

 

Q. What is the method of “mechanical clot detection” → what are the 2 ways to do this?

●      1) Fibrometer method of mechanical clot detection → Two electrodes. One stationary the other moves. Fibrin acts as a conductor of electricity between the two probes and change in conductivity is the endpoint.

●      2) Steel ball method of mechanical clot detection → Magnetically controlled steel ball moves back and forth in the sample. As fibrin forms, viscosity increases, ball motion decreases and the timer is tripped/stopped, signalling clot formation.

 

What is the principle of immunoturbidimetric assay?

 

●      Latex microparticles are coated with antibodies specific to the antigen to be determined.

●      When the latex suspension is mixed with plasma, an antigen–antibody reaction takes place, leading to the agglutination of the latex microparticles.

●      Agglutination leads to an increase in turbidity of the reaction medium and this increase in turbidity is measured photometrically as an increase in absorbance. Usually the wavelength used for latex assays is 405 nm

●      Interferences: Rheumatoid factors and autoantibodies. Give false positive results.

 

What is ACT and ECT and when are they used?

·       Activated clotting time (ACT), used to monitor the effect of high-dose heparin before, during, and shortly after surgeries that require intense anticoagulant administration, such as cardiac bypass surgery, cardiac angioplasty, and dialysis. It is ordered in situations where the PTT test is not clinically useful or takes too long.

·       The ACT is a point- of- care clotting test where whole blood is collected into a tube with a coagulation activator (kaolin, celite or glass particles) and magnetic stir bar. The time for clot formation is measured. It is used in situations where high- dose heparin therapy is needed like cardiopulmonary bypass. The aPTT becomes invalid in such cases.

·       Ecarin Clotting Time (ECT) is a meizothrombin generation test that can be used to measure the activity of the direct thrombin inhibitors such as r-hirudin (lepirudin) and new oral direct thrombin inhibitors.

·       Ecarin directly activates prothrombin to meizothrombin (which has proteolytic activity) and is unaffected by presence of LAC.

 

General sources of error

Q. What patient factors may be a source of error in coagulation testing?

●      Drugs (smoking, caffeine), medications (heparin, DOAC, warfarin)

Q. What collection factors may be a source of error in coagulation testing?

●      Patient position (was patient supine)

●      Tourniquet Time

●      Bore of needle was used (did it cause trauma)

●      Collection from a line (heparin locked?)

●      Collection downstream from an infusion

●      Contamination with EDTA due to improper order of draw

●      Correct number of tube inversions.

●      Inverting the tube (3-4 times)

●      Transport time and temperature (on ice or refrigerated)

Q. What is the correct order of draw for blood specimen (tube type) collection?

●      First - blood culture bottle or tube (yellow or yellow-black top)

●      Second - coagulation tube (light blue top - 3.2% trisodium citrate).

●      Third - non-additive tube (red top)

●      Last draw - additive tubes in this order:

○      SST (red-gray or gold top). Contains a gel separator and clot activator.

○      Sodium heparin (dark green top)

○      PST (light green top). Contains lithium heparin anticoagulant and a gel separator.

○      EDTA (lavender top)

○      ACDA or ACDB (pale yellow top). Contains acid citrate dextrose.

○      Oxalate/fluoride (light gray top)

 

Q. What is the order of draw from a heel poke?

 

CLSI established the order of draw for capillary specimens to be as follows: First — EDTA tubes; Second — other additive tubes; Third — non-additive tubes.

  1. Blood gas
  2. EDTA
  3. Lithium Heparin
  4. Heparin + Gel separator
  5. Na Fluoride
  6. Serum/Clot activator
  7. Serum - No additive
  8. Newborn spot card

Things that don’t seem to be able to be done: Blood Cx and Coags!

 

 

Q. What “handling” factors may be a source of error in coagulation testing?

●      How many times tube inverted, shake tube hard, pneumatic tube system etc

Q. What is the recommended number of tube inversions?

●      Na Citrate 3-4 times

●      Heparin 8 times

●      EDTA 8 times

●      Na Fluoride 8 times

●      Summary: all tubes should be inverted 8 times → except light blue (trisodium citrate coagulation testing tube), which is only inverted 4 times

●      SST 5 times

Q. What “tube type” factors may be a source of error in coagulation testing?

 

●      Tube itself → must use 3.2% trisodium citrate (light blue top tube for coagulation testing)

○      4 tube inversions

●      What type of tube was used, was the tube filled correctly and what is the patient's HCT

○      Correct 9:1 ratio of blood to AC?

●      Polycythemia with Hct >55% requires adjustment of the AC volume

Q. What is the correct trisodium citrate concentration and blood to AC ratio for coagulation testing → what is the ratio for ESR testing?

●      For coagulation studies → use 9 volumes blood: 1 volume anticoagulant (3.2% or 10E9 mmol/l sodium citrate solution)

●      For ESR → use 4:1 ratio (Westergren tube/black top)

Q. What “centrifugation” factors may be a source of error in coagulation testing?

●      Inadequate centrifugation speed or time

○      May lead to incomplete separation of plasma from cells, resulting in platelet contamination (platelet-rich plasma), which can falsely prolong or shorten clotting times.

●      Excessive centrifugation

○      May cause hemolysis or activation of platelets, releasing platelet factor 4 or microparticles, affecting test accuracy (especially in heparin assays).

●      Delay in centrifugation

○      Allows ongoing cellular metabolism, which can alter pH and consume clotting factors (e.g., factor V and VIII degradation), falsely prolonging PT/aPTT.

●      Improper temperature during centrifugation

○      Centrifuging at high temperatures can activate coagulation factors; low temperatures may lead to cold activation of factor VII or cryoprecipitation of fibrinogen.

●      Improper balance of centrifuge

○      Can cause vibration and inadequate plasma separation.

●      Incorrect centrifugation protocol for platelet-poor plasma (PPP)

○      PPP is required for most coagulation assays. Inadequate g-force or time may not sufficiently reduce platelet count to <10,000/µL, affecting results.

Q. What “storage” factors may be a source of error in coagulation testing?

●      Prolonged storage time before testing

○      Labile coagulation factors (e.g., Factor V and VIII) degrade over time, leading to falsely prolonged PT/aPTT if testing is delayed beyond acceptable limits.

●      Improper storage temperature

○      Storing specimens at >24°C can activate clotting;

○      <2°C can cause cold activation of Factor VII or precipitation of von Willebrand factor or fibrinogen, altering results.

●      Repeated freeze-thaw cycles

○      Degrade coagulation factors and activate proteases, especially problematic for frozen plasma aliquots.

●      Incorrect storage of reagents and controls

○      Many coagulation reagents are temperature-sensitive and must be stored as per manufacturer instructions (often 2–8°C or frozen). Expired or poorly stored reagents lead to unreliable results.

●      Inappropriate storage of citrated plasma

○      If plasma is not quickly separated and frozen (for delayed testing), cellular elements may consume or degrade clotting factors.

○      If sample cannot be tested immediately, double spun the specimen before freezing.

●      Use of expired tubes or incorrect storage of collection tubes

○      Can compromise citrate effectiveness and affect calcium chelation.

Q. What are the criteria for rejection of coagulation testing samples?

●      Specimen not properly labeled

●      Compromised tube integrity

●      Hemolyzed sample → free Hb = interference

●      Lipemic sample → lipids = interference

●      Clotted sample → fibrin = interference

●      Samples that are overfilled

●      Inadequately filled tube → relative excess of AC = prolongation of coagulation times

●      Hematocrit > 55% not adjusted → relative excess of AC = prolongation of coagulation times

●      Specimen received > 4 h from collection (The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines (H21-A5) recommend that whole blood samples or plasma samples stored at room temperature for routine hemostasis tests or determination of coagulation factors should be analyzed within 4 hr after sample collection, with the exception of prothrombin time testing with stability up to 24 hr)

Q. What are the considerations for abnormal Hematocrit in coagulation testing and how do you adjust for this?

●      There is no lower limit so you do not adjust for low hematocrit

●      Beyond 55% → you must recollect using a different concentration of AC in your tubes.

●      PT and PTT results are erroneous beyond this point (prolonged due to relative excess of AC to plasma)

●      Same issue exists for underfilled coagulation tubes (less than the 9:1 ratio)

●      Mayo clinic laboratories guideline

     If the patient’s hematocrit is ≥55%, the volume of anticoagulant in the tube should be adjusted.

     If the hematocrit is between 55% and 65%, it is acceptable to remove 0.1 mL of the citrate anticoagulant from the tube and not perform the calculations.

     This will account for most of the patients with high hematocrits, since very few patients will have a hematocrit that is >65%.

     For those patients with hematocrit ≥65%, use the following formula to determine the correct anticoagulant volume:

C = (1.85 × 10-3)(100 - HCT)(V Blood)

     1.85×10−3: A constant multiplier.

     (100−HCT): This subtracts the hematocrit value (which is usually a percentage, so something between 0 and 100) from 100.

     VBlood​: The total blood volume.

Abbreviations: C = volume of citrate remaining in the tube, HCT = patient’s hematocrit, and V = the volume of blood to be added. (If a 5-mL tube is used, V= 4.5 mL)

Example: if Hct is 65, Vblood is 4.5ml, the C is 0.291≈0.3ml

 

Q. Why do we use platelet poor plasma?

●      Platelet membranes (contain phospholipid) are procoagulant surfaces which accelerate coagulation and shorten PT and PTT times

Definition of Platelet rich plasms (PRP) and Platelet poor plasma (PPP).

The platelet content of PRP and PPP is 6 × 1011 platelets/ml and 0.5 × 108 platelets/ml, respectively. 

 

Q. Preactivation of a sample will result in prolongation or shortening of clotting times?

●      Shortened clotting times

Possible scenario

Finding Possible alternate interpretation

Finding Possible alternate interpretation

Clotted specimen

Elevated PT and aPTT

Elevated PT and/or aPTT

Drug effect (heparin, direct thrombin inhibitor, Xa inhibitor); may additionally interfere with the diagnosis of a lupus anticoagulant

Decreased proteins C and S

Warfarin effect; avoid mistaken diagnosis of combined proteins C and S deficiency

Decreased protein S with elevated factor VIII

May not be protein S deficiency, and may be due to high factor VIII causing interference in functional protein S assay

Probable hepatic coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation rather than multiple factor deficiencies

 

Test principles and general principles

In vivo coagulation model

•        In Vivo Coagulation Cascade

•        In in vitro coagulation cascade model, extrinsic pathway is initiated when TF:FVIIa cleaves factor X to Xa

•        Studies of TFPI provide evidence that TF:FVIIa does not cleave factor X to Xa efficiently in vivo﻿

•        TF:FVIIa activation of factor X to Xa reflects what occurs when high concentrations of TF are present (i.e., PT reagent)

•        In vivo, TF:FVIIa has greater activity on factor IX to IXa conversion than factor X to Xa conversion

•        This places factor IX and VIII in a position of greater importance than their placement in intrinsic pathway

•        In vivo, factor XII and proteins HMWK and PK have little to no role in coagulation

•        Factor XI in this model amplifies conversion of factor IX to IXa

•        Factor XI activated to factor XIa by thrombin

•        Remainder of pathway is common pathway with assembly of "tenase" and "prothrombinase" complexes

•        This leads to generation of thrombin and fibrin clot

•        Two-Cell Model

•        Improvement in model of hemostasis incorporates knowledge that 2 cells are present during coagulation

•        TF-bearing cell (e.g., endothelium)

•        Platelets

•        In 2-cell model, 3 processes are needed for fibrin clot formation

•        Initiation

•        Small amounts of activated coagulation factors produced on TF-bearing cells

•        Small amounts of thrombin and factor IXa generated on TF-bearing cells

•        Thrombin and factor IXa available to accelerate coagulation when there is vessel injury

•        When clotting not biologically necessary, thrombin and factor IXa are quickly inactivated or moved to extravascular space

•        Amplification

•        Platelets activated by thrombin generated on TF-bearing cells

•        Factor V released by platelets and activated by thrombin to factor Va

•        Factor VIII activated to factor VIIIa

•        Factor XI activated to factor XIa

•        Factor XI provides supplemental pathway for generating factor IXa for propagation phase

•        All components for generating thrombin in propagation phase now available and "primed" to fully respond

•        Propagation

•        Activated platelets provide phospholipid surface (phosphatidylserine exposure) for coagulation to take place

•        Surface needed for formation of "tenase" and "prothrombinase" complexes on activated platelets

•        "Thrombin burst" generated during this phase

•        Thrombin burst leads to large amounts of fibrinogen being converted to fibrin

•        Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin to form cross-linked fibrin polymer

 

1.aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time)

Q. How do you do an aPTT test?

●      Citrated, PPP sample, add a contact activator (Eg ellagic acid, Kaolin, silica, celite) and partial thromboplastin reagent (PL source) → incubate at 37 degrees for 3-5 minutes.

●      Once incubation is done → add calcium chloride in a 2nd step to initiate clotting and measure the time until clot formation

●      Note → this is a 2 step assay with calcium added in a 2nd step (it is NOT included in the aPTT reagent, whereas the PT is a single step assay with calcium included in the PT reagent with thromboplastin)

●      Clot detection methods → manual (tilt tube method), photo-optical or mechanical[QZ1] 

Q. What are the reagents of aPTT test?

Platelet poor plasma [PPP]

 

Surface activator

Kaolin, Micronized silica, Celite, Ellagic acid

Partial thromboplastin (kaolin or cephaloplastin)

Phospholipid

e.g. Cephalin - to replace platelet phospholipid.  Remember we are using Platelet Poor Plasma [PPP] in this test. The use of a commercial phospholipid substitute e.g. Cephalin means that the test can be standardised.

Calcium

Calcium is required in molar excess for coagulation to occur.
Calcium is removed (by chelation) when blood is collected into sodium citrate and recalcification is necessary to allow coagulation to occur.

 

Q. Why it is called “partial”?

·       The term "partial" refers to the fact that thromboplastin, which is a tissue factor required to initiate the extrinsic pathway, is not included in the test.

·       Instead, only phospholipids and an activator are added, which activate the intrinsic pathway.

 

Q. What is the clotting endpoint measured as (how does this differ between PT and PTT)?

●      The clotting endpoint for all reagents is taken as the first or second derivative peak.

●      Typically:

○      PT uses first derivative peak

○      The first derivative (rate of clot formation) peaks when fibrin polymerization accelerates most rapidly (max slope).

○      PTT uses second derivative peak

○      The second derivative (change in the rate) marks when clot formation transitions from acceleration to stabilization (inflection).

 

 

Q. What are the parts of the clot curve?

 

 

Q. What is the theoretical explanation for a clot curve that is 1) biphasic, and 2) shoulder-type curve shape?

●      1) Biphasic 1st derivative curve → FVIII inhibitor: markedly prolonged peak time and low height of 1st and 2nd DC

○      Possible explanation: Factor VIII inhibitors (autoantibodies) neutralize FVIII, delaying the intrinsic pathway. However, residual thrombin generation via alternative pathways (e.g., extrinsic or common pathway) may trigger a secondary burst of clot formation.

●      2) Biphasic 2nd derivative curve → Hemophilia: markedly prolong peak time of 1st and 2nd DC

○      Possible explanation: In hemophilia A, FVIII deficiency impairs intrinsic pathway amplification. Clotting relies on low-level thrombin generated via the extrinsic pathway, leading to delayed and asynchronous fibrin formation.

●      3) Shoulder-type 2nd derivative curve shape → LAC: prolonged peak time of 1st and 2nd DC

○      Possible explanation: LAC antibodies target phospholipid-protein complexes (e.g., β2-glycoprotein I), interfering with phospholipid-dependent clotting reactions in assays like PTT.

 

Q. What is the name of the PL source used in the PT & aPTT?

●      Cephalin

Q. What are 4 common activators?

●      Celite

●      Kaolin

●      Ellagic acid

●      Micronized silica

Q. What are the 3 contact system factors?

●      Factor XII (Hageman factor), prekallikrein and HMWK.

Q. What do the contact activators do?

●      4 common activators = Celite, Kaolin, Ellagic acid, Micronized silica

●      They provide a → negatively charged surface → to bring the contact system factors in proximity to one another and initiate coagulation through the intrinsic pathway

●      Autoactivation of FXII to FXIIa occurs on a negatively charged surface in the presence of prekallikrein and HMWK.

●      XIIa then activates XI (XII likely plays no significant role in vivo), etc down the intrinsic pathway

●      In vivo XI activation is primarily done by thrombin and not XIIa. In vitro it is activated by XIIa. -> see in vivo model

Q. What is the maximum allowed storage time at room temperature for PTT and PT testing?

●      PT → good for 24 hours at room temperature

●      PTT → good only for 4 hours at room temperature

Q. What factors prolong the aPTT?

●      All clotting factors except VII and XIII

Q. What is your approach to a prolonged PTT (what steps do you initially take to evaluate the cause)?

●      1. Repeat the assay to ensure reproducibility

●      2. Determine whether the patient is receiving heparin or a DTI, or if the sample may have been drawn from a line contaminated with heparin

○      Some laboratories may perform TT and fibrinogen testing at this point

○      Repeating the aPTT with a lupus insensitive reagent (high PL content) may be considered at this stage prior to mixing study too

●      3. If still prolonged, consider mixing study and assess for possibility of inhibitors or deficiencies in the contact pathway (PTT is most sensitive to deficiencies here). Always include an incubated mix to avoid missing a time dependent FVIII inhibitor, even if the initial mix corrects completely

●      Note: If a factor deficiency is suggested by the mixing study then individual factors can be assayed. If there is factor VIII deficiency von Willebrand factor assays should be performed, including a factor VIII binding assay (for Type 2N VWD) or genetic studies.

Q. What are 2 commercially available aPTT reagents - one with high PL content and 1 with low PL content?

●      SynthASil (SLIM = Low PL content → Lupus sensitive):

○      Synthetic phospholipid technology

○      Liquid, ready-to-use

○      Micronized silica activator

○      Sensitive to the contact phase activation

○      Excellent Heparin and Lupus sensitivities

○      LA-sensitive PTT (PTT-LA), one that uses reagents containing low levels of phospholipid

●      SynthAFax (FAT = High PL content → Lupus insensitive):

○      Synthetic phospholipid technology

○      Liquid, ready-to-use

○      Ellagic acid activator

○      Sensitive to Factors VIII and IX

○      Very good Heparin sensitivity → lupus insensitive

○      LA-insensitive PTT (PTT-LAI), one that uses reagents containing high levels of phospholipid

Q. What are causes of a prolonged PTT that don’t convey a bleeding risk?

●      Contact factor deficiency (XII, HMWK, prekallikrein)

○      Typically, aPTT is markedly prolonged >120 sec

●      Lupus anticoagulants

Q. The levels of vitamin K dependent factors are physiologically low at birth. What are 4 factors that contribute to this deficiency?

●      1) Poor placental transfer of vitamin K

●      2) Low vitamin K stores at birth

●      3) Low levels of vitamin K in breast milk [but not in cow’s milk]

●      4) Sterility of the fetal gut

●      Most commercial infant formulas contain supplemental vitamin K and so vitamin K deficiency associated bleeding is almost exclusively a problem of breast-fed infants

●      ICH is uncommon but is the major cause of mortality and long-term morbidity

 

Q. How do DOACS affect the aPTT and PT?

●      PT reagents are more sensitive than PTT.

●      In addition, they show varying sensitivity for the different types of DOAC.

●      PT insensitive to apixaban, but not other types.

●      Dabigatran increases aPTT more than PT/INR, but most significantly increases TT.

●      Riva and Edoxaban can increase PT and aPTT, but no effect on TT.

●      Apix has minimal effect on PT/INR and dose dependent effect on aPTT, but no effect on TT.

Q. How do heparins work?

●      Heparin MOA → potentiates the action of antithrombin III and thereby inactivates thrombin (as well as activated coagulation factors IX, X, XI, XII, and plasmin) and prevents the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin

Q. Three available laboratory tests for monitoring heparin?

●      aPTT, antifactor Xa activity levels (“heparin level”) or ACT depending upon indication

Q. How do you validate a heparin therapeutic range for your PTT?

●      There are 2 methods for determination of a heparin therapeutic range using a particular heparin-reagent-instrument system → the ex-vivo heparin response curve and the in-vitro heparin response curve.

●      1) Ex-Vivo Heparin Response Curve

○      Recommended method for reference methodology → may not be possible for laboratories with a low volume of coagulation testing, because of the large number of blood samples required from patients on therapeutic UFH

○      Samples → individual patient blood samples are acquired from patients who are fully anticoagulated with unfractionated heparin

○      Perform APTT measurements → on fresh plasma aliquots from patient blood samples within 4 hours of collection

○      Perform heparin assay → eg anti-Xa assay (plasma is rendered platelet-free by doubling spinning, frozen, and stored until heparin assays can be performed on a batch of samples). Perform within 1 hour.

○      Graph → the heparin concentration and APTT measurements from each of the test samples are graphically compared

○      Determine therapeutic range → The APTT therapeutic range is determined by reading the applicable APTT range from the graph that corresponds to the therapeutic heparin concentration (0.3 - 0.7 U/ml)

●      2) In-Vitro Heparin Response Curve

○      Not recommended

○      This method is performed more easily and does not require accumulation of samples from patients who are being treated with unfractionated heparin.

○      Samples → a pool of plasma samples is prepared from normal, healthy individuals.

○      Prepare samples → the pool is “spiked” with known concentrations of the particular heparin brand and lot number in use in the facility where the therapeutic range is being calculated.

○      Perform assay → the APTTs of the “spiked” platelet-free, pooled plasma are determined.

○      Graph → the APTT and heparin concentration are graphically compared.

○      The therapeutic APTT range is the APTT range in seconds that correlates with the therapeutic heparin concentration (0.3 - 0.7 U/ml)

●      Heparin therapeutic range: collecting samples

○      ■ >= 30 samples from >= 15 pts on UFH

○      ■ >4 hrs since initiation or change in dose

○      ■ If on warfarin, INR <1.3

○      ■ Should span heparin therapeutic range (0.3 – 0.7 anti-XA U/mL)

○      ■ Spiking NPP with heparin is not recommended

○      – Yields a higher heparin therapeutic range than with ex vivo samples

○      ■ Fresh (<1hr) or freshly frozen samples needed

●     

●      Changing PTT lots

○      ■ CUSUM (cumulative sum of mean differences) is a way of tracking systematic drift that has occurred since the last time the PTT v. anti-Xa relationship was established

○      ■ >= 30 samples are gathered from >15 patients on heparin as before

○      ■ CUSUM is calculated as follows:

○      New CUSUM = Old CUSUM + (∑[New Lot PTT] - ∑[Old Lot PTT])/n

○      ■ ∣CUSUM∣ < 5 or 7sec considered acceptable – sources vary

Q. Three main issues related to aPTT when it is used to monitor UFH:

·       Dose Response Variation: The anticoagulant effect of UFH measured by aPTT can vary due to its binding to different molecules, affecting how it clears from the body.

·       Influence of Coagulation Protein Levels: The effect of heparin on aPTT is influenced by levels of other coagulation proteins like factor VIII and fibrinogen, leading to inconsistent results.

·       Sensitivity of aPTT Reagents: Different aPTT reagents have varying sensitivities to heparin, and without standardization, this can result in significant discrepancies in test results.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.thromres.2017.07.006

 

Q. How do you do an anti-Xa level?

●      Recommended method → use a chromogenic assay with a Xa specific substrate and measure absorbance at 405 nm

●      1) Make a standard curve:

○      Using dilutions of known heparin concentration take plasma, add antithrombin (only some assays do this) and a known amount of Xa

○      Alternatively a series of plasma calibrants of known LMWH concentration can be used.

○      Run the chromogenic assay on each dilution → residual anti-Xa activity is measured using a chromogenic assay and a Xa-specific substrate

○      Plot the results to create the standard curve

●      2) Run the chromogenic assay on your patients sample:

○      Take patients citrated PPP sample, add antithrombin (to account for any deficiency - only some assays use this!!! We don’t), add an excess of Xa (so you can plot against the generated curves),

○      Then run the chromogenic assay

○      Absorbance is proportional to Xa activity, and thus inversely proportional to the amount of heparin

○      The measured anti-Xa activity (drug) is considered to be directly proportional to the plasma drug concentration, whereas the residual Xa activity (serine protease) is inversely proportional to the amount of drug

Q. Using a chromogenic assay, is there increased or decreased light transmission when the chromogenic substrate is cleaved by its serine protease enzyme (eg. FXa)?

●      Clarify with Steven Wong, Todd etc

●      Jason said that if the substrate is p nitroaniline, the cleavage product actually absorbs light, so there is increased OD or decreased light transmission

 

Q. What is the therapeutic range for heparin?

●      The therapeutic range is the spectrum of APTT values that falls between 0.3 and 0.7 IU/mL of heparin

Q. When do we validate the therapeutic range for heparin?

●      Every time there is a new reagent lot of testing component.

●      Should be done using fresh not frozen plasma to ensure residual platelets don't release PF4 (occurs with freezing)

Q. How should we handle plasma samples measuring heparin levels - timing and centrifugation?

●      Sample should be run within 60 minutes

●      Plasma should be double spun to ensure minimal platelet contamination.

Q. How can you manage unfractionated heparin in patients with Lupus anticoagulant?

●      The usual management approach in nonsurgical patients with APS is to switch to low-molecular-weight heparin.

●      In patients in whom heparin remains the agent of choice, management options include:

a.     Monitoring heparin anti-factor Xa levels

b.     Determining an individualized therapeutic aPTT range, targeting an aPTT goal of 2 times the baseline aPTT.

c.     Using an aPTT reagent insensitive to lupus anticoagulant.

2.PT (prothrombin time)

Q. PT reagents

Reagent

Explanation

Platelet Poor Plasma (PPP)

 

Tissue Factor [containing Phospholipid]

Thromboplastin

Tissue Factor binds to FVII and initiates coagulation.
Exogenous phospholipid is used to replace platelet phospholipid

Calcium

Required for re-calcification [- remember the plasma sample is citrated to inhibit clot formation when the blood sample is collected]

 

Q. What factors is the PT sensitive to?

●      FVII and X,  V, II, and fibrinogen (I)

Q. What are the causes of an isolated PT prolongation?

●      Liver

●      Warfarin

●      Vk def

●      Single factor VII def/inhibitor

 

Q. What are 3 things found in a thromboplastin reagent?

●      Tissue factor, phospholipid, heparin neutralizing reagent (polybrene)

Q. Source of heparin neutralization?

●      Polybrene is common and neutralizes up to 1.0 IU/mL

Q. How is the PT performed?

●      Citrated, platelet poor plasma plus thromboplastin reagent (thromboplastin → source of PL, TF & polybrene) AND an excess CaCl2 are all incubated at 37°C

●      Note → this is a 1 step assay with calcium already included in the PT reagent (whereas aPTT adds calcium in a 2nd step)

●      In the manual technique at the same time that the calcium is added, a stopwatch is started and stopped when the clot forms.

●      Clot detection methods: manual (tilt tube method), photo-optical or mechanical

Q. Why is the INR reported instead of the PT

●      PT is dependent on a number of factors including the thromboplastin reagent, instrument and system of measurement (clot detection method)

●      As well, different platforms have different sensitivities to different factor deficiencies.

●      Patients on warfarin tested in different labs in the same city will have different prothrombin times.

●      Sensitivity index refers to variable sensitivity to different factor deficiencies (vit K dependent factors) depending on the thromboplastin reagent used.

Q. What is the INR calculation?

●      [(PT patient)/(PT geometric mean)] ^ISI

●      ISI is experimentally determined by manufacturer and reflects sensitivity of thromboplastin reagent to warfarin dependant factors

Q. What is the international sensitivity index (ISI)?

●      Refers to variable (different) sensitivity to different factor deficiencies depending on your thromboplastin reagent used

●      ISI is experimentally determined by manufacturer and reflects sensitivity of thromboplastin reagent* to warfarin dependant factors* (II, VII, IX & X)

Q. How is the ISI calculated?

●      Normal samples → 20 normal donors not on anticoagulants

●      Abnormals → 60 patients who have been on oral anticoagulant treatment (warfarin) for at least 6 weeks

●      Analyze → Prothrombin Times are performed in duplicate using each thromboplastin (WHO reference and the one being tested)

●      The mean for each pair of tests is derived and plotted (graph)

●      Your ISI = reference ISI x slope of curve

 

Q. Do we calculate the ISI in lab?

·       Most Canadian centres do not validate their own ISI → as international calibrators are not easily available.

·       Instead the ISI is provided by the manufacturer and INR “verification” is done instead

 

Q. What is INR determination/verification?

·       Involves using 1 normal and 3 certified plasmas with known INRs in the therapeutic range of 1.5-4.5.

·       INRs should be within 15% of these plasmas.

·       Otherwise, ISI calibration required

Q. When should PT/INR determination/verification occur?

·       Any change in reagent lot, instrument, major repairs, or abnormal proficiency testing

 

List 4 reasons why the PT wouldn’t rise in the setting of warfarin therapy, excluding poor intake.

·       Noncompliance

·       Excess vitamin K

·       Dosage too low

·       Genetic variations in cytochrome P450 metabolism and altered warfarin receptor

o   CYP2C9 mutation – cytochrome P450 small nucleotide polymorphisms, “slow metabolizers,” greater susceptibility to coumadin

·       FIX propeptide mutation – greater susceptibility to coumadin

·       VKORC1 – gene responsible for recycling vitamin K so it can participate in gamma- carboxylation. Product inhibited by Coumadin. Resistant to coumadin

·       Altered warfarin receptor - Resistant to coumadin

·       Drug interactions:

o   Inhibit warfarin absorption (cholestyramine)

o   Upregulation of P450 system increasing metabolism of warfarin (rifampin, barbiturates, carbamazepine)

 

Elevated PT and PTT

·        Multiple factor def

·        Dic, severe liver, vk def, supratherap warfarin

·        High dose heparin

 

3.Thrombin Time

Q. What are causes of a prolonged thrombin time, and mechanism?

●      Decreased fibrinogen - quantitative abnormality

●      Functional fibrinogen abnormalities - qualitative abnormality

●      Fetal fibrinogen (not as active!)

●      Unfractionated heparin - Indirect Thrombin inhibition

●      Direct thrombin inhibitors - Direct

●      Fibrin split products (May interfere with fibrin polymerisation)

●      Paraproteins (May interfere with fibrin polymerisation)

●      Amyloid (May interfere with fibrin polymerisation)

●      Hypoalbuminemia (unclear mech, in vitro only)

●      Hyperfibrinogenemia (The mechanism is unclear but may reflect interference with fibrin assembly by excess fibrinogen)

Q. What is the clinical utility of the thrombin time?

●      Very little utility as it solely looks at fibrinogen level and function.

●      Given it provides no quantitative level of fibrinogen and functional abnormalities of fibrinogen are extremely rare there is little clinical utility.

●      Reflects the conversion of Fibrinogen to Fibrin but is also sensitive to the presence of inhibitors that may be present in the plasma e.g. heparin.

●      Screen for presence of UFH → causing a prolonged aPTT

Q. TT reagents

Reagent

Explanation

Platelet Poor Plasma (PPP)

 

Human or bovine Thrombin (IIa)

Historically bovine Thrombin was used in this test but this is now frequently replaced by human Thrombin

 

Q. TT methodology?

●      Human Thrombin (or Bovine Thrombin) is added to platelet poor plasma [PPP] at 37°C and the time taken for the formation of a fibrin clot recorded.

●      Recalcification of the plasma is not necessary.

 

Q. What is the use of the reptilase time?

●      Heparin contamination can cause a prolonged PTT.

●      The thrombin time and reptilase time can be used in conjunction to assess this prior to further testing.

●      Inhibitors of thrombin (heparin, DTI dabigatran) will cause prolongation of the thrombin time, but the reptilase time will be normal

Q. Reptilase MOA?

●      Bothrops atrox venom → fibrinogen activator, (uninhibited by antithrombin so unaffected by Heparin)

4.Fibrinogen assay

Q. What are 5 different fibrinogen assays?

 

Assays

Clauss Assay

A functional assay based upon the time for Fibrin clot formation

PT-derived Fibrinogen Assay

A functional assay based upon the time for Fibrin clot formation

Immunological Assay

An immunological method which measures Fibrinogen antigen rather than functional Fibrinogen

Gravimetric Assay

A method based upon clot weight [rarely preformed today]

TEG & ROTEM

The TEG and ROTEM machines can also be used to provide a qualitative indication of the Fibrinogen concentration.

 

Q. Describe the Clauss Method:

 

●      This is a very common method.

●      This is a functional method

●      It is basically a TT clot based assay with VERY high Thrombin

○      Makes it insensitive to heparin effect

●      Citrated, PPP is diluted (typically to 1:10 to dilute) and incubated at 37 degrees with high concentrations of thrombin.

○      Diluted plasma (1:10) is clotted with a high concentration of thrombin.

○      The plasma is diluted (usually 1:10 but this may vary if the fibrinogen concentration is very low or very high) to minimise the effect of 'inhibitory substances' within the plasma e.g. heparin, elevated levels of FDPs

●      The result is plotted against a reference curve created using reference plasma with a known amount of fibrinogen diluted typically to a range of 1:5-1:40. This reference plasma is plotted against the corresponding TT

●      Note: Fibrinogen concentration is inversely proportional to the TT of diluted plasma

 

 

5.D-dimer

 

Q: What is the definition of D-dimer?

·       D-dimer is a soluble fibrin degradation product that results from ordered breakdown of thrombi by the fibrinolytic system.

 

Q. How d-dimer is formed from fibrinolytic process?

·       Thrombin activation: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin monomers.

·       Fibrin polymerization: Fibrin monomers spontaneously polymerize end-to-end to form fibrin protofibrils.

·       Cross-linking by Factor XIIIa: Factor XIIIa, activated by thrombin, cross-links adjacent fibrin monomers at the D domains, stabilizing the fibrin network.

·       Plasmin formation: Plasminogen is converted to plasmin by tissue plasminogen activator, which binds to the fibrin network.

·       Fibrin degradation: Plasmin cleaves the cross-linked fibrin, breaking it down into soluble fragments.

·       D-dimer formation: The degradation produces the (DD)E complex, where two cross-linked D domains (D-dimer) are non-covalently bound to fragment E.

·       Release of D-dimer: Further plasmin-mediated degradation releases fragment E, leaving D-dimer in circulation.

·       D-dimer clearance: D-dimer is eventually cleared from the plasma by the kidneys and reticuloendothelial system

 

Q: What are the main methods for performing a D-dimer test?
The three primary methods are:

  • ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay): A highly sensitive method that uses antibodies to bind and detect D-dimer fragments in a blood sample.
  • Whole Blood Agglutination: Uses bi-specific antibodies to bind D-dimer and red blood cells, causing agglutination in whole blood.
  • Latex Particle Agglutination: Involves latex particles coated with antibodies that bind to D-dimer, forming visible clumps (agglutination).

 

Q: What is the advantage of using the ELISA method for D-dimer testing?

·       ELISA is considered the most sensitive and specific method for detecting D-dimer levels, making it the gold standard in many clinical settings, though it can be more time-consuming than other methods.

 

Q: How does the whole blood agglutination method work for D-dimer testing?

·       This method uses antibodies that are capable of binding both D-dimer and red blood cells. When D-dimer is present in the blood, it causes the red blood cells to clump together (agglutination), indicating a positive result.

 

Q: How does the latex particle agglutination method work?

·       In this method, latex particles are coated with antibodies specific to D-dimer. If D-dimer is present in the sample, it will bind to the particles, causing visible clumping, which is a positive test result.

 

Q: How accurate is the D-dimer test in clinical practice?

·       The D-dimer test is highly sensitive, making it useful for ruling out thrombotic conditions. However, its specificity is low, meaning elevated levels can occur in many other conditions, reducing its effectiveness for confirming diagnoses.

 

Q: Can the D-dimer test be used to definitively diagnose DVT or PE?

·       No, the D-dimer test alone cannot definitively diagnose DVT or PE, particularly in patients with a high pre-test probability. It is best used in conjunction with other clinical assessments and imaging tests to confirm or rule out a diagnosis.

 

6.Factor assays

Q. How do you do factor levels?

●      1-stage APTT based assay (UHT uses lupus insensitive APTT reagent for FVIII FIX FXI FXII)

Reagents

UHT

APTT Reagents: Includes contact activator (e.g., silica, kaolin) and calcium chloride.

HemosIL SynthAFax aPTT reagent

HemosIL SynthAFax CaCL2 solution

Factor diluent

Standard/Reference Plasma: Calibrated against international standards (e.g., WHO reference) to ensure accuracy.

HemosIL Calibration Plasma

FVIII-Deficient Plasma (Substrate Plasma):

    • Commercial or sourced from severe hemophilia A patients (<0.01 IU/mL FVIII, inhibitor-free).
    • Stored at ≤−20°C in aliquots to prevent freeze-thaw degradation.

Precision Biologic Cryocheck

Factor Deficient Plasma:

FVIII, FIX, FXI, FXII

Patient Platelet-Poor Plasma (PPP): Centrifuged to remove platelets and avoid interference.

 

Methodology

  1. Preparation:
    • Pre-warm APTT reagent and CaCl₂ to 37°C.
    • Put patient samples, standard plasma, and substrate plasma on ice to preserve factor activity.
  2. Dilutions:
    • Create 1:10 dilutions of patient and standard plasma in buffered saline.
    • Prepare doubling dilutions (1:20, 1:40) for a calibration curve.
    • For suspected low FVIII levels, use 1:5, 1:10, 1:20 dilutions.
  3. Testing:
    • Mix 0.1 mL of each dilution with 0.1 mL FVIII-deficient plasma.
    • Perform APTT in duplicate, staggered at 2-minute intervals to track clotting times.
    • Include a blank (buffered saline + substrate plasma) as a control.

What is Parallelism?

·       Dilutions are made at 100%, 50% and 25% concentrations.

·       Results of the various sample dilutions are plotted and should demonstrate “parallelism” when compared to the calibration curve of the assay.

 

Why is Factor Parallelism Used?

·       Regulatory bodies recommend a minimum of 3 dilutions of plasma for factors.

·       Increases the quality of the factor assay results.

·       Identifies possible interferences.

·       May be able to dilute out interferences.

 

Criteria to Establish Parallelism:

·       Based on statistical or mathematical analysis of the various plasma dilutions.

·       Compare slope of the curve obtained with test plasma dilutions verses the slope of the calibration curve.

·       Check the variance between the recalculated results of the first sample dilution (100%) and the subsequent dilutions.

·       Check the %CV of CR 100% and %CV of CR

·       %CV = Coefficient of variation

·       CR = Corrected result

 

Q. What is dilutional effect?

·       The dilutional effect in factor assays refers to changes in measured clotting factor activity as a result of serial dilutions of the patient's plasma. This effect is particularly important for detecting the presence of inhibitors—substances (such as antibodies) that can interfere with clotting factors and falsely lower their measured activity at lower dilutions.

Q. What are common sources of error in factor assays?

1. Pre-Analytical Errors

  • Sample Collection:
    • Wrong blood-to-anticoagulant ratio (e.g., underfilled/overfilled tubes).
    • Contamination (e.g., heparin from IV lines, tissue fluid).
  • Handling/Storage:
    • Delays in processing (Factor VIII degrades quickly!).
    • Not freezing samples for long-term storage.
    • Centrifugation issues (platelet contamination).
  • Patient Factors:
    • Medications (e.g., heparin, DOACs, warfarin).
    • Lupus anticoagulant or factor inhibitors (e.g., FVIII antibodies).

2. Analytical Errors

  • Reagents/Instruments:
    • Expired or poorly stored reagents.
    • Instrument calibration/pipetting errors.
  • Test Interference:
    • Cloudy or colored plasma (lipids, hemolysis, bilirubin).
    • High heparin levels (if not neutralized).
  • Method Issues:
    • Discrepancies between 1-step vs. 2-step assays (e.g., with Hemlibra or PEGylated FVIII).

3. Post-Analytical Errors

  • Misinterpretation:
    • Missing inhibitors (e.g., falsely low factor levels).
    • Ignoring clinical context (e.g., patient on anticoagulants).
  • Reporting:
    • Typos, wrong units, or miscommunication.

 

Q. How are two stage factor levels done?

●      Depends on the assay, but be familiar with this methodology.

●      1) 1st stage = generate FXa in a quantity proportional to FVIII concentration

●      2) 2nd stage = assay the FXa and from this derive the FVIII concentration

○      The amount of FXa generated is measured by a clotting-based technique

●      The 2-stage clotting-based Factor VIII assay is less commonly performed than the 1-stage Factor VIII assay and in many labs, the 2-stage FVIII assay has been replaced by the chromogenic FVIII assay.

●      It is becoming particularly important especially with newer factor replacements which cannot be reliably measured using a 1 step assay.

Q. How are chromogenic factor levels done? (protocol from UHT, FVIII chromogenic)

Component

Explanation

Reagent cocktail for generating FXa

Contains FIXa, FX in excess, Thrombin [Factor IIa], a source of calcium ions and phospholipid

Chromogenic substrate

A substance cleaved by FXa to produce a colour change. May also contain a Thrombin inhibitor to stop the FXa generation when the chromogen is added

Patient plasma

Platelet poor plasma

●      First stage, patient plasma is added to a reaction mixture comprised of calcium, phospholipids, purified human thrombin and FIXa and FX of bovine origin. This mixture activates FVIII to FVIIIa, which works with FIXa to activate FX. When the reaction is stopped, FXa production is assumed to be proportional to the amount of functional FVIII present in the sample.

●      Second stage, measure FXa through cleavage of an FXa-specific peptide nitroanilide substrate. The product (pNA) produces a yellow color that can be measured spectrophotometrically by absorbance at 405 nm.

●      The color produced is directly proportional to the amount of functional FVIII present in the sample based on a standard curve.

 

Q. How is the result of the chromogenic assay extrapolated from a reference curve?

●      A reference curve is drawn by plotting the absorbance at 405 nm against concentration on linear graph paper as shown below.

●      For example - if in the case of an unknown plasma sample if the absorbance at 405nm was 0.2 - then from the graph below the concentration of FVIII:C is 56 IU/dl.

 

Q. What are 5 possibilities to explain FVIII deficiency (eg FVIII 0.16 IU/dL) in a female?

  1. Von Willebrand Disease (VWD) eg Type 1. If VWD w/u is normal, always consider type 2N → FVIII binding assay is the test of choice to investigate further for this Dx
  2. Mild Hemophilia A due to a mutation in one of the two F8 genes and Lyonization of the other F8 gene on the other X chromosome → unfavourable lyonization eg associate with Xist mutation
  3. Turners Syndrome (XO) or other karyotypic abnormality affecting one of the two X chromosomes
  4. Inheritance of the 2 separate F8 gene mutations either homozygous or compound heterozygous one on each X chromosome.
  5. Androgen insensitivity i.e. she is XY and has a mutation in the F8 gene

7.Anti-Xa level

Q. What 2 methods are available for anti-Xa level?

·       Chromogenic assay

·       Clotting-based assay

 

Q. How would you do anti-Xa chromogenic assay?

The determination of the Rivaroxaban and Apixaban level in a patient sample is performed by the indirect measurement of direct Xa inhibitor (DXa) as a result of the formation of DXa-FXa complexes, using a chromogenic assay with a colored end-product.

  • The patient plasma containing the DXa is incubated with the chromogenic substrate.
  • After incubation, the FXa reagent (in excess) is added, resulting in the binding of FXa-DXa complexes
  • The unbound, residual FXa, hydrolyses the substrate, releasing pNA (coloured end-product)
  • The quantity of pNA released, measured by absorbance at 405 nm, is inversely proportional to the concentration of DXa in the plasma
  • The more DXa that is present in the sample, the less residual FXa to be detected by the release of pNA (lower O.D.).

 

8.*Bethesda assay*

Bethesda assay was developed to quantify factor VIII inhibitors; Has been expanded for use to quantify other factor inhibitors

 

Q. Define 1 Bethesda Unit (Bu)?

●      The amount of inhibitor in a plasma sample which will neutralize 50% of 1 unit of factor VIII:C in normal plasma after 2hr/120 minutes incubation at 37°C

Q. Bethesda assay basic outline?

●      Bethesda assay - 4 basic steps

a.     Prepare control plasma

b.     Prepare test plasma

c.     Incubate & measure factor level

d.     Calculate inhibitor concentration & derive the inhibitor titer

 

A. The Bethesda assay:

 

●      1. Prepare control plasma

○      Standard assay

■      Control plasma is →

●      1) an equal volume of normal plasma mixed with

●      2) buffer

○      The control is taken to represent the 100% value

●      2. Prepare test (patient) plasma

○      Patient plasma is the source of the inhibitor, which you are diluting out

○      Make doubling dilutions of test (patient) plasma (contains the inhibitor) → [usually 1/2 - 1/1024] in imidazole buffer → then incubate with an equal volume of a normal plasma pool at 37°C.

○      The normal plasma pool will normally contain around 1 IU/ml or 100% factor VIII

○      The inhibitor in the patient sample will → inhibit the corresponding factor in the normal pooled sample

●      3. Incubate & measure factor level

○      At the end of the incubation period (2h 37 degrees) the residual factor VIII is assayed

○      Assay = standard 1-stage aPTT based assay with the control as the 100% (100 IU/dL or 1 IU/mL) standard.

●      4. Calculate inhibitor concentration & derive the inhibitor titre

○      Calculate inhibitor concentration & derive the inhibitor titre

○      Calculated from a graph/chart of residual factor VIII activity versus inhibitor units.

○      Use the chart to determine the Bethesda units of your factor closest to 50% residual → recall the definition of 1 Bethesda unit

○      Then multiply this by the dilution to determine the bethesda units

○      A positive control plasma of known inhibitor titre should be included.

Nijmegen modification

Q. What is the Nijmegen modification - what’s the benefit?

●      Note: 2 things are modified

  1. Buffering the normal pooled plasma NPP (or pooled normal plasma PNP) with 0.1M imidazole buffer at pH 7.4 (normally only the test/patient plasma is buffered with imidazole)
  2. Using immunodepleted factor VIII deficient plasma (imidazole buffer in regular Bethesda) to make the serial dilution of the patient plasma
  3. QZ: in addition, test plasma is heat inactivated to inactivate endogenous FVIII

●      Benefit: can prevent false positives due to inactivation of FVIII due to low pH

UHT protocol

A

Reagent setup

B

Inactivation of patient plasma and QC

1. Place 1mL of citrated patient plasma into a cryovial tube.

2. Thaw one vial of 0.5 mL negative control and two vials of 0.5 mL positive control.

3. Pour thawed negative control into a cryovial tube.

4. Pool and pour thawed positive controls into a cryovial tube.

5. Incubate the sample and QC for 30 minutes at 56 to 58°C in the incubator.

6. Remove from the incubator and centrifuge at 1500g (4000 RPM) for 5 minutes.

7. Remove the clear supernatant and carefully transfer into an aliquot tube.

8. Place on an ice block until ready to test

Table comparing the Bethesda Assay and the Nijmegen Modification step by step:

Step

Bethesda Assay

Nijmegen Modification

1. Prepare Normal Pooled Plasma

Normal pooled plasma (NPP) mixed with buffer, represents 100% factor activity.

Normal pooled plasma buffered with 0.1M imidazole buffer (pH 7.4) to stabilize pH.

2. Prepare Test Plasma

Patient plasma source of inhibitors serially diluted (e.g., 1:2 to 1:1024) with imidazole buffer.

Patient plasma source of inhibitors diluted with Factor VIII-depleted plasma to remove endogenous FVIII.

3. Heat Inactivation

Not performed.

4. Incubation

Equal volumes of diluted test plasma and normal pooled plasma incubated at 37°C for 2 hours.

Same incubation process (2 hours at 37°C).

5. Measure Factor Level

Residual factor activity measured using a 1-stage aPTT assay; control plasma defines 100% activity.

Same measurement of residual activity using a 1-stage aPTT assay.

6. Calculate Results

Residual activity (%R) calculated using formula and converted to BU using a graph or table.

Same calculation, but improved accuracy due to buffering and FVIII depletion.

7. Key Benefits

Simplistic; sensitive to variability and false positives due to pH instability.

Reduced false positives, improved reproducibility, and sensitivity to low-titer inhibitors.

 

9.FXIII assay

Q. What is the traditional method of testing for FXIII deficiency?

●      Clot solubility assay (urea clot lysis test)

●      Demonstrate there is increased solubility of the fibrin clot in

○      5M urea or

○      2% acetic acid or

○      1% monochloroacetic acid 

●      Test method:

○      Clot removed from thrombin-treated plasma samples

○      Clots from affected patient dissolve rapidly (within a few minutes) in 5M/L urea or 1% monochloroacetic acid

○      Clots from normal plasma remain insoluble for 24 hours

○      Test is qualitative and detects only severe factor XIII deficiency

●      Poor sensitivity to mild FXIII deficiencies (.10%) → this test is only positive when concentrations are approximately zero and therefore if patient has been transfused it will be negative or if they have some residual factor XIII the result may be normal → ie only sensitive to severe deficiencies

●      Confirmation is provided by:

○      Immunoelectrophoresis, or

○      Specific assays that measure the enzymatic activity of FXIII

See:https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gRzlwO0ykhNIt9LJppoUkg4oY0TlK91BmzamPXbajUQ/edit#heading=h.iwmhgp4qmyw0

 

Q. What is Amide release assay and how is it done?

·       Amide release assay is a test used to measure the activity of Factor XIII (FXIII) in plasma.

1.     Activation: FXIII is converted into its active form (FXIIIa) by thrombin, which also produces fibrin.

2.     Cross-Linking: FXIIIa cross-links a peptide to glycine ethyl ester, releasing ammonia as a byproduct.

3.     Ammonia Measurement: The released ammonia is detected using a reaction that decreases NADH levels, which is measured at 340 nm. The decrease in NADH is proportional to FXIII activity.

4.     Correction for Errors: To avoid overestimating FXIII activity (especially in severe deficiency), a plasma blanking procedure is used. Here, FXIIIa is inhibited by iodoacetamide to eliminate interference from other ammonia-producing reactions.

Q. What is the clinical manifestation of FXIII deficiency?

·       Bleeding Severity: Correlates with Factor XIII activity levels; less than 1% results in severe bleeding, while over 31% typically keeps individuals symptom-free.

·       Neonatal Symptoms: Up to 80% may experience umbilical stump hemorrhage.

·       Other Symptoms:

o   Hematomas and soft tissue hemorrhage

o   Oral mucosal bleeding (30%)

o   Poor wound healing (30%)

o   Severe bleeding after circumcision in children and recurrent gum bleeding during teething

·        Women’s Symptoms:

o   Menorrhagia (26%)

o   Recurrent spontaneous abortions (66%)

o   Complications like abruptio placenta, preterm delivery, and postpartum hemorrhage

·       Intracranial Hemorrhage: Occurs in up to 30% of cases, often spontaneously, and is a leading cause of death.

·       Alloantibodies: Some patients develop these against Factor XIII after undergoing replacement therapy.

Q. What routine coag tests will show in FXIII deficiency?

·       Normal prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)

·       Normal platelet count

·       Normal thrombin time

·       Normal bleeding time

Ø Biological function of FXIII, urea clot lysis test in FXIII deficiency, 4 clinical manifestations of FXIII deficiency

·       Factor XIII - plasma transglutaminase, catalyzes cross-linking the loose fibrin polymer into a highly organized structure.

·       FXIII is heterotetramer: two catalytic A subunits and two protective/carrier B subunits; activated by thrombin into factor XIIIa; requires Ca2+ as a cofactor.

·       Factor XIII covalently binds fibronectin, a2-plasmin inhibitor, and collagen to the fibrin plug; this enhances adherence to the wound site, resistance to fibrinolysis, and wound healing by providing a scaffold for fibroblast migration and proliferation. Fibrin-fibronectin cross-linking is necessary to support the formation of the cytotrophoblastic shell at the site of placental implantation, which accounts for the role of factor XIII in the maintenance of pregnancy.

·       Other substrates for factor XIIIa, include osteopontin, factor V, thrombospondin, and endothelial cell receptor VEGFR-2 > roles for factor XIII in angiogenesis, atherosclerosis, and inflammation.

·       Congenital Factor XIII deficiency is AR; 1-5/ mln people. Most are due to mutations in the A subunit.

·       Acquired FXIII deficiency: decreased production or increased consumption

o   liver cirrhosis; major surgery; PE; stroke; leukemia; sepsis; DIC;

o   auto-Ab (SLE; malignancies; elderly)

o   detect in mixing study (neutralizing Ab); Bethesda type with Nijmegen modification

o   binding assays (non-neutralizing Ab); IgG (IgM) to purified pFXIII and purified FXIII subunits in ELISA or dot blot assay.

·       FXIII deficiency leads to defective cross-linking of fibrin and vulnerability to late re-bleeds when the primary hemostatic plug is overwhelmed. Bleeding tendencies similar to hemophiliacs develop such as delayed umbilical stamp bleeding (diagnostic of FXIII deficiency), IHC, hemarthroses, deep tissue bleeding and delayed bleeding post-trauma or surgery (12-36 hours) is pathognomonic for F XIII deficiency.

 


Ø Urea Clot Lysis Test – Summary

Purpose & Principle

·        The Urea Clot Lysis Test is a qualitative screening assay for Factor XIII (FXIII) deficiency.

·        FXIII stabilizes fibrin clots by crosslinking fibrin strands and incorporating α2-antiplasmin.

·        Clots formed in the presence of normal FXIII levels remain stable in 5M urea for at least 24 hours.

·        If FXIII is deficient (<2%), the clot dissolves rapidly.

Test Procedure

1.     Plasma Preparation: Platelet-poor plasma (PPP) is mixed with thrombin.

2.     Clot Formation: The mixture is incubated to allow clot formation.

3.     Stability Test: The clot is exposed to 5M urea (or 1% monochloracetic acid) and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours.

4.     Interpretation:

o   Stable clot after 24 hours → Normal FXIII levels.

o   Dissolved clot → FXIII deficiency.

Clinical Interpretation

Result

Interpretation

Clinical Implication

Clot stable for 24h

Normal FXIII function

No FXIII deficiency

Clot dissolves within 24h

Severe FXIII deficiency (<2%)

Congenital or acquired FXIII deficiency (risk of bleeding)

Limitations & Recommendations

·        Not sensitive for mild FXIII deficiencies (detects only <2% FXIII activity).

·        False negatives can occur in recently transfused patients (FXIII from plasma may mask deficiency).

·        False positives can occur in α2-antiplasmin deficiency (clots break down due to unregulated plasmin activity).

·        Urea solubility test is no longer recommended for FXIII screening.

Recommended FXIII Investigations

1.     Functional FXIII activity assay (first-line test).

2.     FXIII antigen testing (to determine FXIII-A vs. FXIII-B deficiency).

3.     Platelet FXIII activity measurement (if plasma FXIII is reduced).

4.     Autoantibody testing (mixing study, binding assays for FXIII autoantibodies).

5.     Molecular genetic testing (to confirm hereditary FXIII deficiency).

6.     Fibrin crosslinking analysis (via SDS-PAGE).

 

Ø Functional assays

·        Enzymatic activity of factor XIII includes measurement of labeled amine incorporation into a fibrin clot

·        measurement of ammonia release during the transglutaminase reaction.

·        Treatment:

·        Plasma-derived FXIII (Fibrogammin P), cryoprecipitate, and rFXIII-A2 concentrates (when become available; being evaluated in clinical trials).

·        Because levels of factor XIII above 5% (10%) are usually sufficient to prevent spontaneous bleeding and because the plasma half-life is long (11-14d), prophylaxis is the management strategy of choice.

·        Prophylactic therapy with factor XIII concentrate 10-20 U/kg every 4-6 weeks

·        severe bleeding; abn wound healing; recurrent miscarriages

·        The half-life of factor XIII is shorter during pregnancy; therefore, treating pregnant patients requires more frequent dosing.

o   250 IU/week in early gestation

o   500 IU/week after 23w GA

o   keep plasma level >30% during delivery (1000 IU booster dose)

 

10.Antithrombin assays

Q. What does antithrombin do?

●      It is a serine protease inhibitor (SERPIN) which inactivates serine proteases including thrombin (IIa), and factors IXa, Xa, XIa, XIIa and VIIa.

●      Gene for AT is SERPINC1 (serine protease inhibitor family C1) located on long arm of chromosome 1

●      It works by forming a covalent bond at the serine site which induces a conformational change to inactivate the target factor

●      Antithrombin is a glycoprotein with a molecular weight of 58 kDa and consists of 432 amino acids. It is encoded by the SERPINC1 gene located on chromosome 1. The protein contains four N-glycosylation sites and three disulfide bonds, which contribute to its structural stability.

●      As a member of the serpin superfamily, antithrombin plays a critical role in inhibiting several coagulation proteases, primarily thrombin (FIIa) and activated factor X (FXa). It also inhibits the FVIIa-tissue factor complex, FIXa, FXIa, and FXIIa. Antithrombin employs a "suicide mechanism" for its anticoagulant activity, which involves proteolytic cleavage of its reactive center loop, trapping the target protease, and undergoing a conformational change to a hyperstable state.

●    

Q. What are some general clinical aspects of antithrombin deficiency?

●      Autosomal dominant inheritance: type 1 (deletion or point mutations) and type 2 (single amino acid substitution -> functional abnormality)

●      Occurs in 0.02-0.17% of general population and 1-5% of patients with VTE

●      Spontaneous thromboembolism is a risk with AT levels of 40-60%.

Q. What are the types of antithrombin deficiency?

●      Plasma AT can be measured both by:

○      Immunological (quantitative) assays, or

○      Functional (qualitative) assays

●      It is on the basis of these assays that antithrombin deficiency is classified as → Type 1 or Type 2.

●      Type I deficiency = Quantitative variants -

○      Associated with a parallel reduction in functional and immunological antithrombin to approximately 50% of normal.

●      Type 2 deficiency = Qualitative variants -

○      Subclassified as follows:

■      Type II HBS: Mutations affecting the heparin binding site (HBS) of antithrombin

■      Type II RS: Mutations that affect the reactive site (RS) of antithrombin

■      Type II PL: (Pleotropic) Mutations that affect both the heparin binding domain and the reactive site of the molecule.

 

Q. How do you do an antithrombin assay? (Chromogenic assay, anti-IIa is more common than anti-Xa based)

1. Incubation with Thrombin and Heparin

  • Platelet-poor plasma (PPP) containing AT is diluted with saline.
  • The sample is incubated with an excess amount of thrombin (FIIa) in the presence of heparin for 90 seconds.
  • AT binds to thrombin, forming an AT-Thrombin-Heparin complex, which inhibits thrombin activity.

2. Detection Using a Chromogenic Substrate

  • A chromogenic substrate (Tos-Gly-Pro-Arg-ANBA-IPA) is added.
  • Any residual thrombin (not inhibited by AT) cleaves the substrate, releasing p-nitroaniline (pNa).
  • pNa produces a color change, which is measured at 405 nm using a photometric method.

Results Interpretation

  • The amount of color change (optical density, OD) is inversely proportional to the AT activity in the sample.
    • Low AT activity → More residual thrombin → More substrate cleavage → Higher absorbance.
    • High AT activity → Less residual thrombin → Less substrate cleavage → Lower absorbance.

Reaction Summary

  1. AT-thrombin complex formation:
    AT sample + Excess thrombin → (with heparin) → AT-Thrombin complex + Residual thrombin
  2. Chromogenic detection:
    Tos-Gly-Pro-Arg-ANBA-IPA + Residual thrombin → Tos-Gly-Pro-Arg-OH + ANBA-IPA (Color change at 405 nm)

 

Q. Acquired Causes of antithrombin deficiency?

●      Decreased synthesis: Liver disease

●      Increased consumption: Sepsis

●      Increased clearance: Kidney disease (e.g., nephrotic syndrome); medications (e.g., heparin)

●      Drugs (heparin, oral contraceptives, L-asparaginase)

11.Protein C and Protein S assays

Q. What does protein C do?

●      Activated protein C degrades factor Va and VIIIa (the 2 cofactors) reducing the rate of prothrombin activation

●      A deficiency in protein C is characterized by the inability to control coagulation, resulting in the excessive formation of blood clots (thrombophilia)

●      Vitamin K dependent

●      Very short half-life 6-8 hours

●      Synthesized in liver

Q. How is Protein C deficiency inherited?

·       Autosomal dominant (AD)(also AD in PS, AT, Prothrombin mutation)

Q. What are 2 types of protein C deficiency?

●      Type 1: 85%; most common; quantitative decrease in normally functioning protein C due to missense or nonsense mutations, promoter mutations, or frameshift deletions or insertions; decreased Pr C Ag and activity levels

●      Type 2: point mutation case qualitative decrease in protein C activity (dysfunctional protein with normal Ag levels)

○      Type 2a: low Pr C activity in both clotting based and chromogenic assay

○      Type 2b:

Q. What are some common causes of acquired protein C deficiency?

●      Decreased synthesis → liver disease, Vit K antagonists

●      Increased consumption → sepsis, DIC, major surgery

●      Severe form of protein C deficiency can be seen in patients with meningococcemia

Q.  What tests are available for Protein C and which should be performed first?

●      Functional assays (activity)

●      Antigen assays (quantitative)

●      Functional assays should be performed first, and if low functional activity is detected, antigen assay should be performed to detect type 2 protein C deficiency

Q. Explain the protein C clot-based functional assay?

●      Patient citrated PPP is incubated at 37°C with a Protein C activator

○      e.g. Protac (Agkistrodon contortrix snake venom, southern copperhead snake)

●      Following incubation with snake venom perform a PT or aPTT.

●      Protein C activity is inversely proportional to time to fibrin formation.

○      Low PC → fast fibrin formation = short time to clot formation

○      High PC → slow fibrin formation = long time to clot formation (prolonged clotting time)

Q. Explain the protein C chromogenic Assay functional assay?

●      Patient citrated platelet poor plasma is incubated at 37°C with a Protein C activator

○      e.g. Protac (Agkistrodon contortrix snake venom, southern copperhead snake)

●      After incubation (typically 5 minutes) a chromogenic substrate for Activated Protein C is added.

●      Absorption or change in optical density is measured

●      By comparison against a standard reference curve, the Protein C level can be determined.

Q. What are issues with functional protein C testing methods?

●      Increased FVIII, decreased protein S, presence of FV Leiden (APCR) & anticoagulant drugs (heparin, warfarin, or DOACs) → will skew results.

Q. Should you use a chromogenic or clotting method to measure protein C activity?

●      Recommendation is to use a chromogenic method.

●      Clotting method has many interferences.

Q. What does protein S do?

●      Cofactor for protein C which increases activity by 10x.

●      Exact mechanism is uncertain.

●      Only free protein S (not bound to C4b-binding protein C4bBP) functions as a cofactor.

Q. How does protein S circulate in plasma?

●      Protein S exists in 2 forms – bound and free.

●      About 65% is in the bound form, complexed to C4b-binding Protein (C4bBP), and is inactive.

●      Only the free form has activity.

●      The proportion of bound and unbound forms is regulated by the availability of C4bBP.

Difference between free and functional protein S, function of protein S

·       Protein S is vit K-dependent co-factor of Protein C in inactivation of FVIII and FV; binds to APC complex.

·       Free (40%) and C4b-bound (60%) in plasma

·       Free protein S-detected by ELISA (unbound to C4b-binding protein, C4BP form) or latex-particle assay

·       Functional-active, detected by functional assay (PT or PTT-based)

·       AD hereditary Protein S deficiency-increased risk of thrombosis

·       Acquired Protein S def: vit-K deficiency; warfarin; pregnancy; liver failure; HIV

Q. Falsely low Protein S

·       Protein S decreases during a thrombotic event. That is why it is important to perform testing for protein S at least 10 days after the event.

·       Protein S is lower in women than in men.

·       Protein S is low at birth but increases to normal range by 6 months of age.

·       Oral contraceptives, estrogen use, warfarin and vitamin K all decrease the level of protein S.

·       In acute phase reactions, C4bBP becomes elevated and binds to and reduces circulating protein S. This makes it appear that there is a protein S deficiency.

Q. What are the 3 protein S mutational types?

●      Type 1 = Quantitative (decreased synthesis)

●      Type 2 = Qualitative (dysfunctional protein S)

●      Type 3 = increased binding affinity to C4bBP (decreased free protein S)

 

Q. How do you measure free protein S antigen - give 2 methods?

●      This requires that the C4bBP-bound Protein S is removed from the assay.

●      This can be achieved either by:

○      1) A pre-assay step that involves precipitating the C4bBP-bound Protein S with PEG.

○      2) An alternative method is to use a monoclonal antibody directed against Protein S epitopes not accessible in the bound form. These are usually the residues that are involved in binding to C4bBP.

Q. Total Protein S Antigen - what are 2 techniques for measuring protein S antigen?

●      Immunological methods → ELISA and Latex particle-based agglutination assays.

●      ELISA is the most commonly used and a number of commercial kits are available.

●      Whatever method is used it must detect Protein S regardless of the level of C4bBP.

Q. Describe APTT-based Functional Protein S Assays

●      Patient citrated PPP is incubated at 37°C with protein S deficient plasma, phospholipid, a contact activator (e.g. Kaolin) and either an excess of activated Protein C or an activator of Protein C (e.g. Protac).

●      After incubation (typically 1-4 minutes) calcium is added to initiate clotting in a 2nd step

●      From this the Protein S level is determined by comparison to a reference curve.

Q. How are latex beads used to measure protein S?

●      In this assay purified C4BP is adsorbed onto the first latex reagent and then incubated with the patient plasma.

●      Free PS is adsorbed on the C4BP latex particle and this triggers an agglutination reaction with the second latex reagent which is sensitized with a monoclonal antibody directed against human Protein S.

●      The degree of agglutination is directly proportional to the free Protein S concentration in the test sample.

Acquired Protein C Resistance APCR

Factor V Leiden Mutation – Summary

Molecular Location & Inheritance

  • Autosomal dominant (AD) with incomplete penetrance
  • Present in ~5% of Caucasians
  • Caused by a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in exon 10 of the F5 gene
  • Arg506Gln missense mutation prevents efficient inactivation of Factor V by activated protein C (APC)

Consequence of Mutation

  • Increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE)
    • Heterozygous: 4–8x increased risk
    • Homozygous: Up to 80x increased risk
  • Prothrombotic state due to APC resistance, leading to prolonged clot formation

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Activated Protein C Resistance Assay
    • Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is determined on patient plasma (APTT pre)
    • Standard amount of APC is added to patient plasma, and APTT is performed again (APTT post)
    • In normal patients, excess of APC favors degradation of factors Va and VIIIa and, therefore, prolongs APTT
    • Patients with APC resistance have little to no change when standard amount of APC is added
    • APC resistance ratio = APTT preaddition APC / APTT postaddition APC
  • APC resistance assay (aPTT-based test)
    • Measures clotting time with and without APC
    • Normal ratio >2.0
    • Heterozygous: 1.5–2.0
    • Homozygous: <1.5
  • Genetic testing (RFLP using Mnl I restriction site)

Clinical Associations

  • Increased risk of VTE, recurrent pregnancy loss
  • Acquired fluctuations in protein S levels (which affects APC function) seen in:
    • Vitamin K antagonist therapy
    • Chronic infections
    • Severe hepatic disease
    • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
    • Myeloproliferative disorders
    • Nephrotic syndrome
    • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Additional VTE risk factors: Oral contraceptives, pregnancy
