c.Hyperhomocysteinemia

Q: What is homocysteine?

  • Homocysteine is a substance made when the body breaks down methionine, an amino acid found in foods like meat, fish, fruits, and nuts.

 

Q: What causes high homocysteine levels?

  • High levels can be caused by genetics, diet, or medications. The most common genetic cause is a deficiency in an enzyme called cystathionine β-synthase. Certain medications, like methotrexate and oral contraceptives, can also raise homocysteine levels.

 

Q: Do MTHFR gene mutations cause high homocysteine?

  • MTHFR mutations are common in White people and rare in Black people, but they don't always lead to high homocysteine levels.

 

Q: How should blood tests for homocysteine be done?

  • The patient should fast before the test, as food affects homocysteine levels. The blood sample must be kept on ice because homocysteine can become unstable at room temperature, leading to incorrect results.

 

Q: What is homocystinuria?

·       A: Homocystinuria is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the homocysteine pathway, most commonly due to a deficiency in the enzyme cystathionine-beta-synthase. It leads to very high homocysteine levels (>100 µM/L) and is associated with a high risk of arterial and venous thrombotic events, often before age 30.

 

Q: What is hyperhomocysteinemia?

·       A: Hyperhomocysteinemia refers to mild to moderate elevation of homocysteine levels, which can result from vitamin B6, B12, or folate deficiencies, renal impairment, or genetic polymorphisms (e.g., in the MTHFR gene). Elevated homocysteine levels are linked to an increased risk of thrombosis, but whether this is causal remains unclear.

 

Q: How does elevated homocysteine contribute to thrombosis?

·       A: Elevated homocysteine can cause endothelial dysfunction, increase oxidative stress, promote platelet aggregation, and trigger vascular inflammation, creating a pro-thrombotic environment. However, lowering homocysteine levels has not been shown to reduce thrombotic risk.

 

Q: What is the role of the MTHFR gene in homocysteine metabolism?

·       A: The MTHFR enzyme helps regulate homocysteine metabolism. Polymorphisms in the MTHFR gene, such as C677T and A1298C, can lead to elevated homocysteine levels. However, in populations with folic acid supplementation, these polymorphisms are not considered significant risk factors for thrombosis.

 

Q: Should homocysteine levels be measured in thrombophilia evaluations?

·       A: No, routine measurement of homocysteine levels is generally not recommended for thrombophilia evaluations, as lowering homocysteine does not reduce thrombotic risk. The exception is in younger individuals (<30 years) with arterial or venous thromboembolism, where there may be suspicion of homocystinuria.

 

Q: Is there a benefit to lowering homocysteine levels with vitamin supplements?

·       A: No, lowering homocysteine levels with B vitamins or folic acid does not reduce the risk of thrombosis, so there is no indication for treating elevated homocysteine solely to reduce thrombotic risk.

 

d.Plasminogen Activator Inhibitor-1 PAI-1

Q. What is PAI-1?

  • PAI-1 is serine protease inhibitor synthesized by endothelial cells and hepatocytes and stored within alpha granules of platelets

 

Q. What does PAI-1 do?

  • PAI-1 is potent inhibitor of plasminogen activators, urokinase plasminogen activator (u-PA) and tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA)
    • Plasminogen activators convert plasminogen to plasmin to promote fibrinolysis by lysing fibrin into fibrin degradation products
    • PAI-1 inhibits formation of plasmin
      • Downregulates fibrinolysis

 

Q. What if the PAI-1 is reduced (PAI-1 deficiency)?

  • Fibrinolysis is increased and may result in bleeding diathesis
  • ﻿PAI-1 deficiency is associated with mild to moderate bleeding

 

Q. What if the PAI-1 is elevated?

  • Elevated PAI-1 is associated with increased risk for venous thrombosis, including VOD after bone marrow transplantation
  • Elevated PAI-1 has also been seen in patients with liver disease, obesity, malignancy, and sepsis

 

e.Protein C deficiency AND Protein S deficiency

See above

 

f.Prothrombin mutation

Q. Laboratory diagnosis of prothrombin mutation is

  • Molecular testing (PCR-based) for detection of 20210A mutation

 

Q. What is the effect of this mutation?

·       gain of function and increased levels of prothrombin

 

g.*Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome*

Definition and criteria

Q. what is APS?

·       Systemic, autoimmune, thrombo-inflammatory disorder

·       Autoantibodies (APLA) target various plasma protein bound to anionic phospholipids

·       Clinical syndrome consistent of various “criteria” and “non-criteria” clinical manifestations

·       Primary or secondary

 

 

APS thrombosis site

·       APS is a prothrombotic disorder that affects both venous and arterial systems.

·       The most common site for venous thrombosis is in the deep veins of the lower limbs, while the most common site for arterial thrombosis is the cerebral arterial circulation.

 

Q. What are antiphospholipid antibodies?

●      Heterogenous group of abs with specificity against human phospholipid-binding proteins.

●      Etiology of why thrombosis occurs in unclear.

●      Presently, three types are recognized as diagnostically important though others exist:

○      Anticardiolipin antibody

○      Anti-beta2-glycoprotein 1 antibody

○      Lupus anticoagulant

What is a lupus anticoagulant?

·       Heterogeneous group of antibodies against phospholipid binding glycoproteins

·       Characteristics:

o   Prolonged phospholipid dependent coagulation abnormality

o   Does not correct with mixing with normal plasma

o   Does correct with addition of excess phospholipids

 

 

Q. What are the clinical criteria for the Sapporo criteria for Dx of APLAS?

●      Clinical criteria – One or more of the following is present:

●      Vascular thrombosis ≥1 clinical episode of arterial, venous, or small vessel thrombosis

●      Pregnancy morbidity

○      a) ≥1 unexplained death of a morphologically normal fetus at ≥10 weeks’ gestation

○      b) ≥1 premature delivery of a morphologically normal fetus at <34 weeks’ gestation because of:  

■      i) Severe pre‑eclampsia or eclampsia defined according to standard definition  

■      ii) Recognized features of placental insufficiency

○      c) ≥3 unexplained consecutive miscarriages at <10 weeks’ gestation, with maternal and paternal factors (anatomic, hormonal, or chromosomal abnormalities) excluded

Q. What are the laboratory criteria for the Sapporo criteria for Dx of APLAS?

●      Laboratory criteria

●      The presence of antiphospholipid antibodies on ≥2 occasions ≥12 weeks apart, identified as one or more of the following:

○      a) Lupus anticoagulant, defined as:  

■      i) Prolongation of a phospholipid dependent clotting test (eg, aPTT or dilute Russell viper venom test);  

■      ii) Evidence for an inhibitory effect in patient plasma (eg, mixing with normal plasma does not correct the prolonged clotting time as would be expected for a simple factor deficiency); and  

■      iii) Evidence that the inhibitory activity can be quenched via the addition of excess phospholipids

○      b) Moderate to high titer anticardiolipin antibodies of IgG or IgM isoforms, defined as >40 (moderate) to >80 (high) GPL or MPL units, or greater than the 99th centile, determined by the laboratory providing the test

○      c) Moderate to high titer anti‑β2GPI antibodies of IgG or IgM isoforms, defined as greater than the 99th centile, determined by the laboratory providing the test

 

Q. What is the laboratory definition of a lupus anticoagulant?

●      A phospholipid dependent prolongation of a clotting time

○      This corrects with addition of phospholipid or with a non-PL dependent (PL insensitive) test

●      Understanding this is fundamental and key to understanding the different laboratory investigations used to identify a LAC - underscore this point!

●      In general, lab testing compares a PL dependent (sensitive) test to a non-PL dependent test → use a ratio

Effect of Anticoagulants on Testing

Moll S. J Thromb Thrombolysis 2015 (39):367-378

 

ISTH Criteria for LAC

○      Positive screening test (phospholipid-dependent coagulation assay) with two or more screening tests (DRVVT and aPTT)

○      Evidence of inhibition in mixing test (exclude factor deficiency). 

○      Evidence that inhibition is phospholipid-dependent (neutralization of LAC by excess phospholipid)

○      Exclusion of coagulation inhibitors (heparin, DOAC, factor VIII inhibitor)

 

●     

●      Fritsma G, et al. Hematology Clinical Principles and Applications. Chapter 42.  2012.

●      Pengo V, et al. J Thromb Haemost 2009; 7(10):1737-1740

Lab testing for LAC

Q. How many methods of identifying LACs should labs offer?

●      They should offer 2

●      If positive by either method the patient is considered to have a LAC

●      Only 1 method may show positivity

Q. Name 5 different methods that can be used to demonstrate a LAC?

  1. aPTT (various reagent sensitivities)
  2. DRVVT
  3. Silica clotting time
  4. STACLOT assay
  5. Dilute thromboplastin inhibition assay
  6. FV ratio
  7. Textarin:Ecarin ratio

Q. What are the screening tests and what are the confirmatory tests for LAC?

·       Screen

o   aPTT

o   DRVVT

·       Mixing studies

o   aPTT

o   DRVVT

·       Confirmatory tests

o   DRVVT confirmatory

o   Hexagonal phospholipid neutralization

 

Q. What constitutes APLA workup at Unity Health Toronto?

·       The APLA panel includes all testing below:

·       Lupus sensitive aPTT

·       DRVVT

·       ACA IgG

·       ACA IgM

·       Anti-B2GP1 IgG

·       Anti-B2GP1 IgM

·       Hexagonal phospholipid (STACLOT)

Q. How would you investigate lupus anticoagulant at UHT?

·       PT/INR,

·       aPTT-SS (moderately sensitive to LA), aPTT-SP (markedly sensitive to LA) and DRVVT

·       Run thrombin time (TT) if aPTT-SS and/or aPTT-SP is prolonged

·       Run aPTT-SS 50/50 mix if aPTT-SS is ≥40 seconds

·       Run aPTT-SP 50/50 mix if aPTT-SP is ≥40 seconds

·       If aPTT-SS and/or aPTT-SP is prolonged but less than 40 seconds, order the 50/50 mix, but enter the comment: “aPTT result is not significantly prolonged. 1:1 mixing studies not indicated.”

·       Run fibrinogen if PT/INR and aPTT-SS/aPTT-SP is prolonged

·       The Staclot/hexagonal phospholipid assay will only be ordered under the directive of the Medical Director

Q. UHN protocol

DRVVT,

·       If normal, no further testing is required, negative

·       If prolonged, perform DRVVT mix, DRVVT confirm, PT/INR, TT, TTC if TT is prolonged

·       If DRVVR mix corrects, the DRVVT ratio will not be calculated, negative

·       If DRVVT mix is prolonged, DRVVT ratio will be calculated

·       If DRVVT ratio is negative, negative

·       If DRVVT ratio is positive, positive

Ls-PTT,

·       If normal, no further testing is required, negative

·       If prolonged, perform Ls-PTT mix, PT/INR, TT, TTC if TT is prolonged

·       If Ls-PTT mix corrects, no further testing is required, negative

·       If Ls-PTT mix is prolonged, if DRVVT ratio is negative, perform Staclot test

·       If DRVVT ratio is positive, and TT is normal, I

·       If DRVVT ratio is positive, and TT >120 and TTC <21, possible UHF contamination, LA result be cancelled

·       If DRVVT ratio is positive, and TT/TTC both prolonged, possible DTI contamination, LA results be cancelled

 

Q. What can interfere with laboratory testing of lupus anticoagulant?

·       Patients with factor deficiencies, on oral Vitamin K Antagonists, unfractionated heparin (UFH), low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), thrombin inhibitors or Factor Xa inhibitors may exhibit false positive results.

·       The dRVVT Screen/dRVVT Confirm results are not affected by hemoglobin up to 200 mg/dL, bilirubin up to 10 mg/dL, triglycerides up to 500 mg/dL, unfractionated heparin (UFH) and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) up to 1 U/mL.

a.STACLOT hexagonal phospholipid

Q. What is the STACLOT assay?

●      A hexagonal phase phospholipid neutralization procedure used as a confirmatory assay for the detection of lupus anticoagulants (LAC).

●      Hexagonal-phase phospholipids neutralize LAC, reversing clotting prolongation.

●      The STACLOT-LA can detect the presence of a lupus anticoagulant in patients on heparin and/or Coumadin.

HPE = hexagonal phospholipid

 

b.dRVVT

Q. How is the dilute Russell viper venom test (DRVVT) done?

●      Pt citrated PPP sample + a direct activator of factor X (Daboia russelii snake venom), which in the presence of phospholipid, prothrombin, and calcium will convert fibrinogen → fibrin.

●      The test is run twice.

○      A low (diluted) phospholipid concentration = screen test

○      A high phospholipid concentration (+PL) = confirmatory test (aka the neutralization test)

●      Advantage: It is insensitive to most factor deficiencies

●      Results are reported as a ratio → [Test DRVVT/control DRVVT] => see later UHT protocol

●      Ratio >1.05 [QZ5] suggests possible LAC (factor deficiencies still possible) → next step is to perform the correction test by adding PL

Q. What are two sources of phospholipid for the correction test?

●      Platelets

●      Phospholipid concentrate - e.g. Cephalin

○      Cephalin is any of several phosphatides/phospholipids occurring in animal tissue cell membranes, especially of the brain, and having marked blood-clotting properties.

Q. What are 2 ways to calculate the percentage correction?

·       A number of approaches have been used to calculate the percentage correction:

o   Using the formula below where '+PL' is the dRVVT with additional phospholipid i.e. the neutralisation step.

o  

o   A normalised correction The percentage correction of the ratio is calculated using the formula below where again '+PL' is the dRVVT with additional phospholipid. The final result is multiplied by 100 to covert it into a percentage.

o  

o   Note: This is simply: (screen ratio - correction ratio) / screen ratio

·       This latter calculation is that currently recommended by the British Committee for Standardisation in Haematology [BCSH.]

Q. What constitutes a positive DRVVT correction ratio?

●      Most laboratories regard a correction of >10% with PL as being a positive test

Q. What factors does Russell viper venom activate?

●      FX

●      Some references say it also activates factors V and II to some extent.

Q. What are causes of false positive DRVVT?

●      Deficiencies of factor V could prolong the DRVVT although the ratio should not be changed (eg Test DRVVT/Test DRVVT + PL → the test DRVVT would be prolonged in each case and the ratio unaffected by the FV deficiency)

●      Drugs → DOACs, heparin, and possibly warfarin.

●      This method (DRVVT) relies on optical clot detection → so all interferences that would impact that detection method can throw results off (hemolysis, hyperlipidemia, hyperbilirubinemia)

Q. What are considerations when handling samples for DRVVT testing?

●      It is important to ensure the sample is double spun → so that residual platelets don’t provide phospholipid (PLTs should be < 10 x 10^9/L for double spun samples)

The ratio for dRVVT Screen is calculated as follows:

The ratio for dRVVT Confirm is calculated as follows:

The ratio result from the dRVVT Screen is divided by the ratio result from the dRVVT Confirm:

Q. What is the reference interval for Normal ratio in Unity Health?

·       <1.17

 

Q. What are the differences between normalized dRVVT ratio and percentage correction?

1. Purpose:

  • Normalized dRVVT Ratio:
    • Used to compare the clotting times of the patient's plasma in both the screen and confirm steps of the dRVVT.
    • It helps identify the presence of LA by adjusting for phospholipid sensitivity, with the confirm step reducing the effects of LA.
    • A higher normalized ratio suggests that the patient's clotting time is prolonged due to the presence of LA.
  • Percentage Correction:
    • Used to measure how much mixing with normal plasma or phospholipids corrects the clotting time.
    • It calculates the percentage improvement in clotting time after mixing, indicating the neutralization of LA.
    • A higher percentage correction indicates that the clotting time has improved significantly after mixing, suggesting the presence of LA.

2. Calculation:

3. What They Reveal:

  • Normalized dRVVT Ratio:
    • Shows the degree of interference caused by LA in the patient's plasma by comparing clotting times before and after the confirm step.
    • A high ratio suggests the presence of LA because the confirm test (with added phospholipids) corrects for the LA's interference.
  • Percentage Correction:
    • Measures the extent to which the LA’s effect can be neutralized by mixing the patient's plasma with normal plasma or additional phospholipids.
    • A higher correction percentage indicates that the LA is causing the prolonged clotting time, as the mixing helps neutralize this effect.

c.Textarin to ecarin ratio

Q. What is the principle of the textarin to ecarin ratio?

 

●      Compares a PL dependent test to a non-PL dependent test

●      Textarin and Ecarin = both are snake venoms that both activate Factor II (prothrombin)

●      Textarin is phospholipid dependent and Ecarin is not

○      Textarin:

■      Requires Factor V, PL, and Ca2+ to activate prothrombin → Thrombin

■      Will be prolonged in the presence of a PL dependent inhibitor (i.e. LAC)

○      Ecarin:

■      Directly activates prothrombin → to meizothrombin (which has proteolytic activity)

■      Unaffected by presence of LAC

●      Therefore an elevated ratio (Textarin / Ecarin) is consistent with a LAC (i.e. Textarin is prolonged but not Ecarin)

d.FV ratio

Q. How does the factor V ratio work?

●      Similar to the Textrarin:Ecarin ratio

●      aPTT-based Factor V assay → Uses low phospholipid (PL) content – lupus sensitive

●      PT-based Factor V assay → Uses high phospholipid content – non lupus dependent

●      Factor V Ratio = (aPTT-based Factor V Level​)/(PT-based Factor V Level)

○      A prolongation suggests LAC present (PL-dependent inhibition)

e.Dilute thromboplastin inhibition

Q. What is the dilute thromboplastin inhibition assay?

●      A test based upon the PT, rarely performed today

●      Thromboplastin = a source of PL (and TF)

●      Diluting the Thromboplastin reagent in a PT-based assay, increase its sensitivity to a LA

●      As you dilute, the phospholipid (PL) in the reagent will decrease → making it more susceptible to prolongation of the clotting time by a lupus anticoagulant

●      Compares a PL dependent test to a non-PL dependent test. The ratio of the clotting time with the dilute thromboplastin [1:500] divided by the normal reagent [1:50] is compared to a normal control.

●      Report results as a ratio → compares a PL dependent (low PL in diluted thromboplastin) test to a non-PL dependent (high PL) test

●      Increased ratio is indicative of a LAC. A PT ratio ≥1.3 suggests the presence of a LA whilst a ratio ≤1.1 is considered normal.

●      The DTI is not a LA screening test that is recommended by the ISTH. The tests that are recommended are the Silica Clotting Time [SCT] and the dRVVT assay.

APS variants (pregnancy, high risk, catastrophic)

Q. What are the three types of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (classification)?

●      Primary

●      Secondary

●      Catastrophic

Q. What is the difference between primary and secondary APLAS?

●      Primary → the patient has no associated disease.

●      Secondary → the patient has another associated disorder (most commonly SLE/lupus). (30% SLE has aPLs.)

Q. What are the criteria for catastrophic APS?

1. Evidence of involvement of three or more organs, systems, and/or tissues

2. Development of manifestations simultaneously or in less than a week

3. Confirmation by histopathology of small vessel occlusion in at least one organ or tissue

4. Laboratory confirmation of the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant and/or anticardiolipin antibodies)

Definite catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome

• All four criteria

Probable catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome

• All four criteria, except for only two organs, systems, and/or tissues involvement

• All four criteria, except for the absence of laboratory confirmation at least six weeks apart due to the early death of a patient never tested for antiphospholipid antibodies before the catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome

• 1, 2, and 4

• 1, 3, and 4 and the development of a third event in more than a week but less than a month, despite anticoagulation

 

Catastrophic APLA, diff Dx from TTP on PB

o  The term ‘catastrophic’ antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an accelerated form of APS resulting in multiorgan failure.

a)  clinical evidence of multiple organ involvement developed in a very short period of time

b)  histopathological evidence of multiple small vessel occlusion (a minority also have large vessel thrombosis)

c)   laboratory confirmation of the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL), usually in high titer

d)  most of the catastrophic APS episodes are preceded by a precipitating event, mainly infections.

o  < 1% of all patients with APS;

o  the mortality rate is approximately 50% despite treatment

o  the optimal treatment regimen is unknown (anticoagulation, plasma exchange, especially if evidence of MAHA, schistocytes in PB)

 

 

Q. What is the role of rivaroxaban in the treatment of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome?

 

●      There was no increase in thrombotic risk compared with standard-intensity warfarin, this drug could be an effective and safe alternative in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome and previous venous thromboembolism.

●      Cohen H, Hunt BJ, Efthymiou M, Arachchillage DR, Mackie IJ, Clawson S, Sylvestre Y, Machin SJ, Bertolaccini ML, Ruiz-Castellano M, Muirhead N, Doré CJ, Khamashta M, Isenberg DA; RAPS trial investigators. Rivaroxaban versus warfarin to treat patients with thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome, with or without systemic lupus erythematosus (RAPS): a randomised, controlled, open-label, phase 2/3, non-inferiority trial. Lancet Haematol. 2016 Sep;3(9):e426-36. doi: 10.1016/S2352-3026(16)30079-5. PMID: 27570089; PMCID: PMC5010562.

●      Note: Not to be used for triple-positive APLAS patients, as there is a higher risk of thrombosis

o   Pengo V, Denas G, Zoppellaro G, Jose SP, Hoxha A, Ruffatti A, Andreoli L, Tincani A, Cenci C, Prisco D, Fierro T, Gresele P, Cafolla A, De Micheli V, Ghirarduzzi A, Tosetto A, Falanga A, Martinelli I, Testa S, Barcellona D, Gerosa M, Banzato A. Rivaroxaban vs warfarin in high-risk patients with antiphospholipid syndrome. Blood. 2018 Sep 27;132(13):1365-1371. doi: 10.1182/blood-2018-04-848333. Epub 2018 Jul 12. PMID: 30002145.

Studies showed conflicting results. Most recent meta-analysis concluded DOACs are not effective in all APS patients and should not be used routinely in these patients. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/treatment-of-antiphospholipid-syndrome/abstract/63

Q. What is the rule on blood donation and lupus anticoagulant?

●      If diagnosed with LA, you are no longer eligible to donate.

Q. Why is it important that the PT be insensitive to lupus anticoagulant?

●      Patients with lupus anticoagulant are often anticoagulated with warfarin → need to be able to monitor warfarin with the INR

●      Therefore PT has a high PL content → rarely, a strong LAC may prolong the PT and INR

Q. What is the significance of the different types of antiphospholipid antibodies in pregnancy?

●      The PROMISSE study showed:

○      LAC is the primary predictor of adverse pregnancy outcome

○      Anti-cardiolipin antibodies & Anti-beta2-glycoprotein 1 don't predict a poor outcome in pregnancy.

○      Arthritis Rheum. 2012 Jul; 64(7): 2311–2318.

●      APLS in pregnancy (Blood, March 2012)

o   Autoimmune disorder presented with venous and arterial thromboses and/or obstetric complications in the presence of persistent APLA (LAC, aCL, anti-β2-GpI)

o   purely obstetric APLS (diagnosed during pregnancy with no previous Hx)-higher risk of VTE (1-7%) even with low dose aspirin prophylaxis

o   heterozygous FVL and prothrombin G20210A gene mutation-not at increased risk compared to non-thrombophilic women

o   LAC-the most powerful predictor of thrombosis (titre-depended)

 

Q. What is a general approach to anticoagulation in pregnant patients?

 

●      Warfarin is teratogenic → 1st choice in non-pregnant patient but NOT in pregnancy

●      LMW heparin is an agent used in pregnancy

○      If at very high risk (ie. recent thrombosis within 3 months) administer treatment dose LMWH and bridge with UFH prior to expected delivery

○      If low risk (primary prophylaxis), administer lower prophylactic dose LMWH and discontinue LMWH prior to delivery without bridging

●      If fully anticoagulated, delivery should be planned:

○      High-risk centre

Q. What is high risk APS?

·       Various definitions exist but the most widely accepted high risk characteristics are ‘triple positivity’ (positive for LA, aCL and anti-beta2 glycoprotein-I) or a history of arterial thrombosis.

·       Some also consider a history of small vessel thrombosis or organ involvement, heart valve disease according to Sydney criteria, or recurrent thrombosis as high risk characteristics.

α-Granules

Q. Describe platelets

●      Not true cells → cytoplasmic fragments of megakaryocytes

●      Formed in the bone marrow → circulate in the blood.

●      They bind to vWF via GPIb-IX-V or directly to collagen in the subendothelium via GPIa/IIa (collagen receptor)

●      Activated platelets → become negatively charged providing a surface for the coagulation cascade to occur on as well as increased availability of GPIIb/IIIa.

●      Primary hemostasis = formation of the PLT plug

●      Serotonin

●      Pyrophosphate

●      P selectin

Q. What is ARC syndrome

●      Arthrogryposis-renal dysfunction-cholestasis (ARC) syndrome

●      Rare but fatal autosomal recessive (AR) multisystem disorder caused by mutations in

○      VPS33B gene (15q26.1), involved in intracellular protein trafficking and membrane fusion, have been found in 75% of ARC families

○      VIPAR gene (C14ORF133), encoding a protein that complexes with VPS33B

●      The classical presentation of ARC includes congenital joint contractures, renal tubular dysfunction, and cholestasis

●      Most patients die within the first year of life despite supportive care for metabolic acidosis and cholestasis and those surviving longer show cirrhosis and severe developmental delay

Q. What is a disorder associated with thrombocytopenia and small PLTs?

●      Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)

Q. What are 4 disorders associated with large platelets (macrothrombocytopenia)?

●      Bernard Soulier syndrome (GP1bA, GP1bB & GP9 genes)

●      MYH9-related disorders (Myosin-9, aka myosin, heavy chain 9 gene)

●      Paris-Trousseau syndrome (11q chromosome deletion. FLI1 = candidate gene)

●      X-linked macrothrombocytopenia

 

Q. Describe some features of Chediak-Higashi Syndrome?

●      Mutation of lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST) gene on chromosome 1

●      AR inheritance

●      Many clinical features:

○      Partial oculocutaneous albinism

○      Peripheral neuropathy

○      Decrease in phagocytosis → results in recurrent pyogenic infections

○      Pancytopenia

○      HSM, lymphadenopathy

○      Lymphoid transformation of EBV infection

○      HLH in accelerated disease

●      Fusion of granules in leukocytes → large chunky granules

Q. Describe the MYH9 related disorders?

●      Mutations in the gene encoding the heavy chain of the non-muscle myosin-9 (MYH9)

●      Autosomal dominant (AD)

●      40% have minor bleeding

●      Phenotype determined by localization of the mutation.

●      Common features → macrothrombocytopenia, renal disease (glomerulonephritis), sensorineural deafness, cataracts, dohle-like inclusion bodies in all leukocytes.

○      May-Hegglin anomaly

○      Epstein syndrome → absent dohle-like inclusions

○      Fechtner syndrome → thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, sensorineural hearing loss, and kidney and ocular abnormalities

○      Sebastian syndrome → thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, sensorineural hearing loss, cataracts, and renal involvement

●      Epstein syndrome lacks leukocyte inclusions. If Alport syndrome-like features (deafness, cataracts, and nephritis) are suspected, an audiogram, renal function testing (creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, proteinuria) and ophthalmologic examination should be performed. Both Epstein and Fechtner syndromes have clinical characteristics similar to Alport syndrome. Ultrastructural features of leukocyte inclusion bodies differentiate Sebastian syndrome from MHA. MHA does not have limiting membrane on electron microscopy and shows ribosomes clusters oriented along the axis of thin parallel filaments. In contrast, Sebastian syndrome has ribosomes but without parallel filaments depolymerized ribosomes.

●   Untanu RV, Vajpayee N. May-Hegglin Anomaly. [Updated 2023 Jul 17]. In: StatPearls [Internet]. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing; 2025 Jan-. Available from: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441952/

Q. Describe the blood film features of May-Hegglin Anomaly?

●      Prominent “Dohle like bodies” → present in all leukocytes (granulocytes, lymphocytes, and monocytes)

●      Poorly granulated giant platelets and variable thrombocytopenia (40% have minor bleeding)

●      Absent in Epstein subtype

Q. Compare toxic vs May-Hegglin anomaly Dohle bodies?

●      Toxic Dohle bodies:

○      Peripheral

○      1-2 um

○      Granulocytes/neutrophils only

●      May-Hegglin anomaly “Dohle like bodies”:

○      2-5um

○      Random distribution, sometimes between nuclear lobes

○      Present in all leukocytes (granulocytes, lymphocytes, and monocytes)

May Hegglin anomaly – genes, mode of inheritance

o  MHA is associated with the MYH9 gene encoding for nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA (MYH9). AD inheritance. Unique cytoplasmic inclusion bodies are aggregates of nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA, and are only present in granulocytes. MYH9 is also found to be responsible for several related disorders with macrothrombocytopenia and leukocytes inclusion, including Sebastian, Fechtner, and Epstein (no inclusions) syndromes, which feature deafness, nephritis, and/or cataract.

 

Q. Describe some features of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

●      An X-linked disorder (WAS gene is on X chromosome)

●      Severe immunodeficiency, small platelets (microthrombocytopenia), and eczema

●      Bloody diarrhea (secondary to the thrombocytopenia)

●      Sometimes called the eczema-thrombocytopenia-immunodeficiency syndrome

●      Mnemonic: TIE (thrombocytopenia, immunodeficiency, eczema)

Q. What are the 3 WAS related disorders?

●      Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

●      XL Thrombocytopenia (XLT)

●      X-linked congenital neutropenia (XLN)

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

o  Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is a rare X-linked recessive disease characterized by eczema, thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), immune deficiency, and bloody diarrhea (secondary to the thrombocytopenia). It is also sometimes called the eczema-thrombocytopenia-immunodeficiency syndrome in keeping with Aldrich's original description in 1954. The WAS-related disorders of X- linked thrombocytopenia (XLT) and X-linked congenital neutropenia (XLN) may present similar but less severe symptoms and are caused by mutations of the same gene (different mutations).

o  The type of mutation to the WASp gene correlates significantly with the degree of severity: those that led to the production of a truncated protein caused significantly more symptoms than those with a missense mutation but a normal-length WASp. Although autoimmune disease and malignancy occur in both types of mutation, those patients with truncated WASp carry a higher risk.

o  The first signs of WAS are usually petechiae and bruising, resulting from thrombocytopenia. Spontaneous nose bleeds and bloody diarrhea are common. Eczema develops within the first month of life. Recurrent bacterial infections develop by three months. Splenomegaly is common. The majority of WAS children develop at least one autoimmune disorders, and malignancies (mainly lymphoma and leukemia) develop in up to 30% of patients.

o  IgM levels are reduced, IgA and IgE are elevated, and IgG levels can be reduced or elevated.

 

 

Q. Describe some features of Paris-Trousseau/Jacobsen syndrome - what gene is affected?

●      Autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia.

●      Have facial and cardiac defects

●      Psychomotor retardation

●      Macrothrombocytopenia

●      Alpha granule deficiency

●      11q chromosome deletion of the gene encoding the transcription factor friend leukemia integration 1 (FLI-1)

Q. Describe the clinical features of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS). Name 2 genes involved

●      Oculocutaneous albinism, a bleeding diathesis, and, in some individuals, pulmonary fibrosis with restrictive lung disease, granulomatous colitis, or immunodeficiency with neutropenia.

●      Clinical findings of hypopigmentation of the skin and hair, characteristic eye findings, and demonstration of absent delta granules (dense bodies)

●      Genes: HPS, AP3, BLOC1S (each followed by different numbers)

 

Describe platelet functions in hemostasis

1.     Adhesion and aggregation forming the primary haemostatic plug

2.     Clot retraction

3.     Release of platelet activating and procoagulant molecules

4.     Provision of a procoagulant surface for the reactions of the coagulation system

 

Steps

·        Adhesion:

  • Vessel injury exposes the subendothelial matrix - collagen and basement membrane.
  • VWF binds to exposed collagen and captures platelets by attaching to the GPIb receptor.
  • Platelets adhere to the injured vessel wall, forming a monolayer.

·        Activation and Shape Change:

  • VWF binding to GPIb triggers platelet activation through a G-protein mechanism.
  • Platelets undergo a shape change:
    • From disc-shaped to spherical.
    • Pseudopods (projections) extend to increase surface area for interactions.
  • Activated platelets release ADP, 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), and thromboxane A2, which enhance further platelet activation.

·        Aggregation:

  • Platelets stick to one another to form a platelet plug.
  • Fibrinogen, fibronectin, and VWF facilitate aggregation by binding to the GPIIb/IIIa and GPIbIX glycoprotein complexes.
  • This results in increased cell-to-cell contact, stabilizing the growing platelet mass.

·        Release of Granules and Feedback Loop:

  • Platelets release granules containing ADP, 5-HT, and thromboxane, which further activate and recruit more platelets.
  • In areas of nonlinear blood flow (near injury), damaged red cells release ADP, amplifying platelet activation.

·        Formation of the Platelet Plug:

  • The aggregate of platelets forms a stable platelet plug that seals the damaged vessel.
  • This plug is later strengthened by fibrin from the coagulation cascade, ensuring effective blood clotting and preventing excessive bleeding.

 

Classification of Thrombocytopenia

a.ITP

 

 

b.TTP and HUS

Q. What is the definition of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura TTP?

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a rare and lifethreatening thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) defined by a severe deficiency in ADAMTS13 (A Disintegrin and Metalloprotease with ThromboSpondin type 1 repeats, member 13), the specific von Willebrand factor (VWF)-cleaving protease.

 

Q. What are the differential diagnosis of TTP?

Other TMAs

  • Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)
  • Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS)

Non-TMA Conditions

  • Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)
  • Evans syndrome
  • Hematologic malignancies
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

 

Q: What is the structure of VWF?
A: VWF is arranged as SP-D1-D2-D'-D3-A1-A2-A3-D4-C1-C2-C3-C4-C5-C6-CK domains. Pre-pro-VWF contains a 22-amino acid signal peptide, a 741-amino acid propeptide (D1-D2), and a 2050-amino acid mature subunit

 

Q: Where is VWF synthesized and stored?
A: VWF is synthesized in vascular endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. It is stored in Weibel-Palade bodies of endothelial cells and in α-granules of platelets and megakaryocytes

 

Q: What are the key functions of VWF in hemostasis?
A: VWF functions as a carrier protein for factor VIII in circulation, binds to collagen types I and III, and recruits platelets to injured vessel walls by binding to platelet glycoprotein Ibα and integrin αIIbβ3

 

Q: How is VWF regulated under high shear stress conditions?
A: High shear stress induces a conformational change in VWF from a globular to an elongated form, exposing binding sites for platelet glycoprotein Ibα and ADAMTS13

 

Q: What is the genetic location and plasma characteristics of VWF?
A: The VWF gene contains 52 exons and covers 178 kb on chromosome 12p13.3. In plasma, VWF concentration is approximately 10 µg/mL with a half-life of about 12 hours

 

Q: How does VWF contribute to the pathophysiology of TTP?
A: In TTP, severe ADAMTS13 deficiency leads to accumulation of ultralarge VWF multimers in the blood. These ultralarge multimers promote spontaneous formation of platelet-rich microthrombi in small arterioles and capillaries, causing widespread microvascular ischemia

 

Q: What does ADAMTS13 stand for?
A: ADAMTS13 stands for A Disintegrin and Metalloprotease with ThromboSpondin type 1 repeats, member 13.

 

Q: What is the main function of ADAMTS13?
A: ADAMTS13 is the specific von Willebrand factor (VWF)-cleaving protease. It cleaves the Tyr1605-Met1606 bond in the VWF A2 domain, regulating VWF multimer size.

 

Q: What is the structure of ADAMTS13?
A: ADAMTS13 consists of a metalloprotease domain, a disintegrin-like domain, a first thrombospondin type 1 repeat (TSP1), Cys-rich and spacer domains in the N-terminal region, and seven additional TSP1 repeats and two CUB domains in the C-terminal region.

 

Q: Where is ADAMTS13 produced?
A: ADAMTS13 is produced by hepatic stellate cells, podocytes and renal tubular epithelial cells, platelets, and endothelial cells.

 

Q: What are the plasma characteristics of ADAMTS13?
A: In plasma, ADAMTS13 concentration is approximately 1 µg/mL and its half-life is about 2-3 days.

 

Q: How does ADAMTS13 conformation change in TTP?
A: ADAMTS13 adopts an open conformation at the acute phase of acquired TTP, exposing a cryptic epitope in the spacer domain. During remission, it returns to a folded conformation.

 

Q: What is the clinical significance of ADAMTS13 deficiency?
A: Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency leads to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). This can be congenital (due to biallelic ADAMTS13 gene mutations) or acquired (due to anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies).

c.DIC

 

d.HIT

Q. Etiology

Immune-mediated disorder, formation of antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4)/heparin complex

 

Q. How often does HIT occur in heparin treated patients?

1-5% of patients treated with heparin for >= 4 days

 

Q. How often does HIT patient develop thrombosis? When will occur?

30-50%; occur 2-4 weeks after heparin is discontinued.

 

Q. The mortality rate of thrombosis-related HIT?

5%

 

Q. Types of immune-mediated HIT?

Typical HIT (type 2)

Delayed-onset HIT

Persisting HIT

Heparin “flush”-induced HIT

Fondaparinux-associated HIT

Spontaneous HIT

 

Q. HIT clinical probability scores

4T score

 

A score of ≤3 indicates a low pretest probability for Type II HIT [<5% chance of HIT]

A score of 4–5 indicates an intermediate risk.

A score ≥6 is associated with a very high risk of HIT.

 

The American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) Guidelines for the diagnosis of Type II HIT has identified the following diagnostic criteria:

 

     1. Thrombocytopenia - a fall in platelet count that occurs 4–10 days after beginning heparin therapy

     2. A fall in platelet count to <150 x 109/L or to <50% of the baseline platelet count

     3. The exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia

     4. The recovery of the platelet count to >90% of the baseline platelet count after heparin is stopped.

 

Remember not all patients with HIT will develop a thrombosis. The following diagram illustrates this:

A significant number of individuals may come up positive with an ELISA assays that detects a variety of antibodies some of which are non-pathological but only a small number will detect clinically significant HIT.

 

Q. Laboratory tests for HIT

A number of tests exist for the detection of antibodies in suspected cases of HIT and these can be either functional tests or immunological tests.

1.     Immunological assays detecting antibodies against PF4 complexed with heparin (or heparin-like substrate) (FDA-cleared assays available)

·       Immunoassays:

o   Particle gel immunoassays (PaGIA)

o   ELISA

o   Latex particle-enhanced assays

·       Chemiluminescent assays

2.     Functional

·       SRA (gold standard)

·       Platelet aggregation assays

·       Flow cytometry: HIT Alert, PEA

Q. What is the mechanism of HIT?

●      IgG antibodies are formed against heparin/platelet factor 4 complexes and cause activation and degranulation of platelets via FCgamma IIa receptors

●      Platelet Factor 4 (PF4) Binding to Heparin:

○      Platelet Factor 4 (PF4), a protein released by platelets, binds to heparin to form a complex.

●      Immune Complex Formation:

○      The PF4-heparin complex is recognized as foreign by the immune system, leading to the production of IgG antibodies.

○      These IgG antibodies bind to the PF4-heparin complex, forming immune complexes.

●      Fc Receptor Activation:

○      Immune complexes bind to Fc receptors on platelets.

○      This triggers platelet activation and aggregation.

●      Consequences:

○      Thrombocytopenia: Activated platelets are removed by splenic macrophages, leading to a drop in platelet count.

○      Thrombosis: Platelet activation causes the release of procoagulant microparticles, enhancing clot formation, which can result in venous or arterial thrombosis.

 

Q. What are the 4 T's of HIT?

●      Thrombocytopenia

●      Timing

●      Thrombosis

●      AlTernative possible causes

 

Q. Draw the 4T score diagram!!

 

Q. Explain the 4T score risk stratification for HIT

●      Low score 0-3

○      NPV = 0.998

○      Do not do HIT assay

●      Intermediate score 4-5

○      PPV 0.14

■      Still very low, this means 14% will have HIT

○      Do HIT Assay

■      If negative test, then not likely HIT

■      If positive result, can still be false positive

●      High score 6-8

○      PPV 0.64

○      Anticoagulation change indicated

■      Treat empirically

○      Do HIT Assay

■      If test is negative, will order further testing (i.e. SRA) to ensure not false neg

Q. What are two anticoagulants that can be used in cases of HIT?

●      Direct thrombin inhibitors → Argatroban, bivalirudin

●      Indirect factor Xa inhibitors → Danaparoid, fondaparinux

 

Q. What are the options for HIT testing?

●      Polyspecific (IgG/IgA/IgM) ELISA

●      IgG ELISA (Traditionally)

●      PaGIA gel column

●      HemosIL AcuStar (poly- and IgG specific)

●      HemoSIL Hit-Ab (PF4-H)

Q. Explain the ELISA based HIT assay?

●      PF-4/polyvinyl sulfate complex →  mimics PF4/heparin complex (polyvinyl sulfate substitute for heparin)

●      Add patient serum sample → HIT antibodies will bind the PF-4/polyvinyl sulfate complex

●      Incubate and wash

●      An enzyme labelled AHG is added, which will bind the HIT antibodies

●      Incubate and wash

●      Detection → an enzyme substrate is then added, which is cleaved by the enzyme.

 

Q. Explain the competitive latex agglutination HIT assay

 

●      Latex particle agglutination

○      1) Latex bead coated with HIT like antibody and (antibody with specificity for the PF4/heparin complex)

○      2) PF4/Polyvinyl sulphate (PVS) complex (mimics PF4/heparin complex)

●      Competition between 1) latex bead coated with anti-HIT antibody and 2) PF4/PVS complex for the HIT antibody in patients serum

●      Presence of HIT antibody in patients serum will compete for the PF4/PVS complex and there will be decreased agglutination & decreased absorbance

■       Less agglutination = more positive!!!

○      <1.0 = negative, >1.0 = positive

■      Based on currently available evidence of at least 95% and specificity of 75% at the 1.0 U/mL cutoff

■      For results >4.0 u/mL, specificity is the 95%

 

 

Q. What is the principle of SRA?


Mix the following 3 things:


1) Donor platelets loaded with [14C] serotonin
2) Heparin

●      Use multiple concentrations

○      100U/mL heparin - very high, will overwhelm and should not have platelet activation

○      0.1-0.5 U/mL heparin - more similar to a patient concentration of heparin

3) Patient serum (contains anti-heparin-PF4 complex antibody)


The percentage of serotonin released is then measured.

 

 

 

Q. What is the cutoff for a positive SRA result for HIT?

 

●      Cutoff for positive results → ≥ 20 % serotonin release with low dose heparin but <20% with high dose heparin = represents platelet activation and a positive result

●      The SRA is 95% sensitive and specific but the test is technically complex and less readily available for immediate management decisions.

●      Considered the gold standard among diagnostic tests for HIT

Q. What is the principle of flow cytometry in HIT?

●      Flow cytometry

○      Patient plasma mixed with platelets, to see if patients plasma will activate platelets

○      Increased platelet expression of P-selectin (CD-62P)

○      Anionic Phospholipids

○      Not widely used

Ø FIX dosing: each u/kg increases FIX level by 1%; high risk of anaphylactic reaction:

Ø Lyophilized FXI concentrate: each FXI U/kg increases factor level by 2.4%; high risk of thrombosis; also could use DDAVP and tranexamic acid to control mucocutaneous bleeding

 

 

 

7.Inhibitors of Coagulation

 

a.TFPI Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor

Q. What is TFPI?

·       A single-chain polypeptide protease inhibitor which can reversibly inhibit Xa and Factor IIa (thrombin).

·       While Xa is inhibited, the Xa-TFPI complex can subsequently also inhibit the FVIIa-TF complex. TFPI contributes significantly to the inhibition of Xa in vivo. Found in vascular endothelium and plasma in free and plasma lipoproteins-bound form.

 

Q: What is the primary function of Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor (TFPI)?

·       TFPI inhibits the early phases of blood coagulation by blocking the TF–factor VIIa (fVIIa) complex and the prothrombinase complex (fXa–fVa).

·       TFPI is the first major inhibitor to act, rapidly inhibiting the TF-VIIa complex (which initiates coagulation).(Dacie)

 

Q: How does TFPI inhibit the TF–factor VIIa complex?

·       TFPI inhibits the TF–factor VIIa complex by first binding to factor Xa (fXa) and then forming a complex that blocks the activation of downstream clotting factors.

 

Q: What are the two major isoforms of TFPI and where are they located?

·       The two major isoforms of TFPI are TFPIα, which is found in plasma and platelets, and TFPIβ, which is anchored to the surface of endothelial cells.

 

Q: What role does TFPI play in preventing excessive clot formation?

·       TFPI prevents excessive clot formation by inhibiting the TF–fVIIa and prothrombinase complexes, limiting thrombin generation and reducing the risk of unnecessary thrombus formation.

 

Q: What is the significance of TFPI in hemophilia treatment?

·       Pharmacological inhibition of TFPI can restore thrombin generation and hemostasis in patients with hemophilia, offering a potential treatment for this bleeding disorder.

 

b.Antithrombin (AT)

Q: What is the primary function of AT:

·       Antithrombin (AT) is the principal inhibitor of thrombin (Factor IIa) in plasma.

·       It also inactivates other coagulation factors like FXa, FIXa, FXIa, and FXIIa, although with lesser efficiency.

 

c.Thrombomodulin

Function of thrombomodulin

·       Thrombomodulin, CD141 is an integral membrane protein expressed on the surface of endothelial cells. Thrombomodulin functions as a cofactor in the thrombin-induced activation of protein C by forming a 1:1 complex with thrombin.

·       Thrombomodulin-bound thrombin has no procoagulant effect (unable to cleave fibrinogen).

·       Thrombomodulin binds thrombin and facilitates its clearance by ATIII

·       The TT-complex inhibits fibrinolysis by cleaving thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI) into its active form.

 

Q: What is the primary function of thrombomodulin (TM) in hemostasis?

·       Thrombomodulin binds to thrombin, converting its role from procoagulant to anticoagulant by promoting the activation of protein C.

·       As thrombin moves away from the injury site, it binds to thrombomodulin, a protein on the endothelial surface. (Dacie)

 

Q: How does thrombomodulin inhibit thrombin's procoagulant activity?

·       Thrombomodulin binds thrombin, which prevents it from activating fibrinogen and clotting factors V and VIII and instead activates protein C to degrade factors Va and VIIIa.

 

Q: What is the role of activated protein C (APC) in thrombomodulin-mediated anticoagulation?

·       APC, activated by the thrombomodulin-thrombin complex, inactivates clotting factors Va and VIIIa, reducing thrombin generation and inhibiting clot formation.

 

Q: How does thrombomodulin contribute to the regulation of fibrinolysis?

·       Thrombomodulin enhances the activation of thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI), which decreases fibrinolysis by reducing plasminogen binding to fibrin.

 

Q: What effect does thrombomodulin have on thrombin’s ability to activate platelets?

·       Thrombomodulin inhibits thrombin's ability to activate platelets, reducing platelet aggregation and preventing excessive clot formation.

 

Summary: (Dacie)

The body has multiple inhibitory mechanisms to regulate coagulation and prevent excessive clot formation:

  • TFPI quickly inhibits the TF-VIIa complex.
  • Antithrombin inactivates thrombin and other coagulation factors.
  • Thrombomodulin bound thrombin activates protein C, which further limits coagulation by inactivating Va and VIIIa with the help of protein S.
  • These systems ensure the clot is localized to the injury site and prevents uncontrolled clotting throughout the vasculature.

8.Fibrinolysis

Q: What is fibrinogen, and what is its role in coagulation?

  • Fibrinogen is a soluble protein present in plasma at concentrations of 200-400 g/L.
  • It plays a critical role in blood clot formation by being converted into fibrin, the main structural component of a blood clot.
  • Fibrinogen is also an acute-phase reactant, meaning its levels increase during stress, inflammation, or pregnancy.

 

Q: How is fibrinogen structured?

  • Fibrinogen consists of two sets of three polypeptide chains (Aα, Bβ, and γ), which are linked by disulfide bonds. These chains form a triglobular structure with a central E-domain and two peripheral D-domains.

 

Q: What triggers the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin?

  • The enzyme thrombin, generated during the coagulation cascade, cleaves two small peptides from fibrinogen: fibrinopeptide A (FPA) and fibrinopeptide B (FPB). This cleavage exposes binding sites, leading to the formation of fibrin monomers, which polymerize to form an insoluble fibrin clot.

 

Q: How does thrombin contribute to clot stabilization?

  • Thrombin not only cleaves fibrinogen but also activates factor XIII into factor XIIIa. Factor XIIIa cross-links the fibrin polymers, creating a stable, durable clot that is resistant to fibrinolysis.

 

Q: What is fibrinolysis, and why is it important?

  • Fibrinolysis is the process of breaking down a blood clot once it has served its purpose. It prevents excessive clot formation and clears clots when they are no longer needed. Fibrinolysis is initiated by tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), which activates plasminogen to form plasmin, an enzyme that digests fibrin into fibrin degradation products (FDPs).

 

Q: What are D-dimers, and what do they indicate?

  • D-dimers are a specific type of FDP that are released when cross-linked fibrin (stabilized by factor XIIIa) is broken down by plasmin. The presence of D-dimer in the blood is evidence that thrombin has acted on fibrinogen to form fibrin, the fibrin has been cross-linked, and fibrinolysis has occurred.

 

Q: How is fibrinolysis regulated?

  • Fibrinolysis is tightly regulated by natural inhibitors to prevent excessive clot breakdown. These inhibitors include plasminogen activator inhibitors (PAI-1 and PAI-2), which block tPA activity, and α₂-antiplasmin, which directly inactivates plasmin.

 

Q: What are the consequences of hyperfibrinolysis?

  • Hyperfibrinolysis occurs when there is excessive clot breakdown, leading to a risk of bleeding. Common causes include disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), liver disease, trauma, or conditions like urothelial carcinoma that increase urokinase production.

 

Q: What causes hypofibrinolysis, and what are the clinical consequences?

  • Hypofibrinolysis occurs when fibrin clots are not broken down effectively, increasing the risk of thrombosis. This can result from conditions like liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, or hypothyroidism, which alter the levels of fibrinolytic enzymes and their inhibitors.

 

Q: What is the role of urokinase (uPA) in fibrinolysis?

  • Urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA) is another activator of plasminogen, primarily acting on soluble fibrinogen. Unlike tPA, which is more effective on the fibrin surface, uPA is found in the plasma and subendothelial tissues and plays a significant role in conditions with increased fibrinolysis, such as urothelial cancer.

 

Q: What is clot lysis time, and what does it measure?

  • Clot lysis time is a global test of fibrinolysis, which measures the time required for a fibrin clot to break down after the addition of exogenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) to platelet-poor plasma. It reflects how long it takes for the fibrinolytic system to dissolve a clot.

 

Q: What does an increase in clot lysis time indicate?

  • An increase in clot lysis time suggests hypofibrinolysis, meaning the body’s ability to break down clots is impaired, which can increase the risk of thrombosis (excess clot formation).

 

Q: Can clot lysis time predict hyperfibrinolysis?

  • Clot lysis time is not as predictive for hyperfibrinolysis (excessive clot breakdown) and is better suited for detecting reduced fibrinolysis (hypofibrinolysis).

 

Q: What is thromboelastography (TEG), and how does it work?

  • Thromboelastography (TEG) is a test that measures the viscoelastic properties of clot formation in whole blood. The device tracks the mechanical strength of the forming clot by measuring the amount of torque required to rotate a pin or cup in the sample as the clot forms.

 

Q: What does TEG measure in clot formation?

  • TEG assesses:
    • The time to initiate clot formation (clotting time).
    • The maximum strength of the clot, which reflects both platelet function and fibrinogen activity.
    • The time to clot lysis, as measured by the decrease in clot strength after reaching the maximum, which reflects fibrinolysis.

 

Q: How does TEG provide information on platelet and fibrinogen activity separately?

  • Specific inhibitors of platelets can be added to a TEG sample, allowing the maximum clot strength to reflect only fibrinogen activity. This isolates fibrinogen’s contribution to clot formation.

 

Q: Why is TEG useful in clinical practice?

  • TEG provides real-time, dynamic information about the entire process of clot formation and breakdown in whole blood, helping clinicians assess both coagulation (how well the blood clots) and fibrinolysis (how well the clot is broken down). It is especially valuable in managing patients with bleeding or clotting disorders, during surgery, or in trauma settings.

 

Q. How is plasminogen activation regulated?

·       Thrombin-Activated Fibrinolysis Inhibitor (TAFI):

·        Activated by thrombomodulin-bound thrombin.

·        Removes amino-terminal lysine residues from fibrin, which prevents plasminogen and tPA from binding to fibrin, thus inhibiting plasmin activation.

 

Q. What are the inhibitors of the Fibrinolytic System?

  • Plasminogen Activator Inhibitor-1 (PAI-1):
    • A potent inhibitor of tPA and uPA.
    • Produced by endothelial cells, platelets, hepatocytes, and placenta.
    • Serpin family member that controls fibrinolysis by preventing plasminogen activation.
    • Plasma levels vary and play an important role in regulating the fibrinolytic process.
  • Plasmin Inhibitor (α2-Antiplasmin):
    • The main physiological inhibitor of plasmin in plasma.
    • Forms a 1:1 complex with plasmin, preventing its action.
    • This reaction occurs rapidly in free solution but is prevented when plasmin is bound to fibrin within the clot.

 

3 physiologic inhibitors of fibrinolysis

·       Plasminogen activator inhibitor I and II (PAI-1, PAI-2) – inhibits tPA, uPA

·       alpha-2 antiplasmin – inhibits plasmins

·       thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI) – protects fibrin from fibrinolysis

Laboratory Testing of Fibrinolysis:

Biochemical structure of fibrin – why D-dimer test is more specific test for fibrin degradation than the FDP

·       Fibrinogen molecules are comprised of two sets of disulfide-bridged A-alpha-, B-beta-, and gamma- chains. Each molecule contains two outer D domains connected to a central E domain by a coiled- coil segment. Fibrin is formed after thrombin cleavage of fibrinopeptide A (FPA) from fibrinogen alpha-chains, thus initiating fibrin polymerization. Double-stranded fibrils form through end-to- middle domain (D:E) associations, and concomitant lateral fibril associations and branching create a clot network. Fibrin assembly facilitates intermolecular antiparallel C-terminal alignment of gamma-chain pairs, which are then covalently 'cross-linked' by factor XIII ('plasma protransglutaminase') or XIIIa to form 'gamma-dimers'. In addition to its primary role of providing scaffolding for the intravascular thrombus and also accounting for important clot viscoelastic properties, fibrin(ogen) participates in other biologic functions involving unique binding sites, some of which become exposed as a consequence of fibrin formation.

·       D-dimer detects cross-linked fibrin degradation product

 

FDP test

·       Principle

o   latex particles with specific Ab to FDP fragments D and E will aggregate in the serum with FDP; testing different dilutions - semiquantitative assay

·       Reagents

o   Blood sample in a special test tube (antifibrinolytic agent and thrombin); test kit; pos and neg controls (from manufacturer)

·       Method

o   Allow to clot > serum in dilutions + latex suspension > glass slide > agglutination

·       Interpretation

o   agglutination with 1:5 dilution = FDP>10μg/ml

o   1:20 =FDP>40 (in systemic fibrinolysis: DIC and thrombolytic therapy)

o   Normal <10

o   10-40 seen in DVT, MI, pneumonia, after major surgery

 

Q1: What is the Euglobulin Lysis Time (ELT), and how is it used to assess fibrinolysis?

Definition & Purpose:

  • ELT (also called ECLT) is a screening test for fibrinolysis.
  • It measures how quickly a clot formed from the euglobulin fraction of plasma breaks down.

Test Procedure:

  1. Blood Collection: Venous blood is drawn into tubes containing trisodium citrate (anticoagulant).
  2. Plasma Preparation: The sample is centrifuged, and the plasma is separated.
  3. Precipitation Step: Acetic acid is added to precipitate plasminogen, plasminogen activators, and fibrinogen, while the supernatant is discarded.
  4. Clot Formation: The precipitate is dissolved in a buffer, and thrombin is added to induce clot formation.
  5. Clot Lysis Time Measurement: The time it takes for the clot to dissolve is recorded.

Interpretation:

ECLT (minutes)

Fibrinolysis Status

Clinical Implications

< 60 min

Hyperfibrinolysis

Seen in DIC, liver disease, thrombolytic therapy

90–240 min

Normal

No significant fibrinolysis abnormality

> 240 min

Hypofibrinolysis

Seen in thrombotic disorders with reduced fibrinolysis

Limitations:

  • ELT is non-specific and does not identify the cause of hyperfibrinolysis.
  • Results vary between laboratories due to different protocols.

 

Q2: How does α₂-Antiplasmin (α₂AP) regulate fibrinolysis?

  • α₂-Antiplasmin is a natural inhibitor of plasmin, the enzyme responsible for breaking down fibrin clots.
  • Low levels of α₂AP lead to excessive plasmin activity, causing excessive fibrinolysis and bleeding.
  • α₂AP levels are measured by assessing its ability to inactivate a known amount of plasmin.

 

Q3: What is the role of Plasminogen Activator Inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) in fibrinolysis testing?

  • PAI-1 inhibits tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) and prevents the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, thus regulating fibrinolysis.
  • PAI-1 is measured by a functional assay with chromogenic endpoints.
  • Low levels of PAI-1 may cause excessive fibrinolysis and bleeding, though most assays are better suited to detect high levels, which are linked to thrombosis.

 

Q4: How is Tissue Plasminogen Activator (TPA) measured, and what does it indicate?

  • TPA can be measured using a functional assay, which tracks its ability to convert plasminogen to plasmin.
  • TPA antigen can also be measured by ELISA.
  • Increased levels of TPA may be seen when PAI-1 is low, leading to excessive fibrinolysis and bleeding.

 

Q5: What is Thrombin Activatable Fibrinolysis Inhibitor (TAFI), and how is it measured?

  • TAFI is a protein that regulates fibrinolysis by inhibiting the breakdown of clots.
  • It can be measured functionally or immunologically, and its activated form, TAFIa, can also be assessed.
  • TAFI serves as a marker of thrombin generation and the role of thrombin in controlling fibrinolysis, though its clinical significance is still being investigated.

 

Q6: How is fibrinogen measured, and why is it important in fibrinolysis?

  • Fibrinogen levels can be measured easily and help determine the effectiveness of fibrinolytic therapy.
  • During treatments like TPA therapy, fibrinogen levels typically decrease to about 50% of normal.
  • Maintaining fibrinogen levels above 100 mg/dL is important to reduce bleeding risk.

 

Q7: What do Fibrin Degradation Products (FDPs) indicate in fibrinolysis?

  • Fibrin Degradation Products (FDPs), including fragments D and E, indicate the breakdown of fibrin and fibrinogen.
  • FDP assays use latex agglutination to detect these fragments.
  • D-dimer is a particularly useful marker because it indicates that cross-linked fibrin was formed by Factor XIIIa, and its presence suggests the formation and breakdown of a stable clot.

 

Q1: What is the clinical purpose of the D-dimer test?
A: The D-dimer test is used to help rule out thrombotic disorders like deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).

 

Q2: Why is the D-dimer test important for diagnosing venous thromboembolism (VTE)?
A: It has a high negative predictive value, meaning a low result can effectively exclude VTE, reducing the need for more invasive tests.

 

Q3: Can the D-dimer test confirm a diagnosis of DVT or PE?
A: No, an elevated D-dimer alone cannot confirm DVT or PE. It must be used in conjunction with other clinical assessments and imaging tests.

 

Q4: What conditions, other than VTE, can raise D-dimer levels?

·       Pregnancy

·       HELLP

·       DIC

·       Snake bites

·       Malignancy

·       Surgery/trauma/burns

·       VTE

·       Etc.

 

Q5: How is the D-dimer test used in clinical decision-making?
A: The test helps rule out VTE in patients with low clinical suspicion, but elevated levels require further diagnostic testing like ultrasound or CT.

 

False positive D-dimer tests (latex agglutination)

·       D-dimer concentrations may rise in the elderly, and false positives may be seen with high levels of  rheumatoid factor, a protein seen in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Substances such as high triglycerides, lipemia, and bilirubin can also cause false positives as can hemolysis caused by improper sample collection and handling.

 

 

Ø 3 tests to evaluate the fibrinolytic system

·     Chromogenic assay for fibrinogen - two-step amidolytic assay (plasminogen + streptokinase > plasmin-like activity on plasmin-specific peptide > dye released proportional to amount of plasminogen)

·     streptokinase-plasminogen complex is not inhibited by the plasma plasmin inhibitors

·     Plasminogen concentration reduced- newborn, cirrhosis, DIC, thrombolytic therapy (assay less reliable; high levels of fibrinogen or fibrin degradation products may augment plasmin activity)

·     Plasminogen concentration increased- acute phase reactant (infection, trauma, MI, cancer)

·     Euglobin lysis time - diluted and acidified plasma precipitates, forms euglobulin (tPA, plasminogen, fibrinogen); most of the plasmin inhibitors left in the solution

·     Precipitate is re-dissolved, fibrinogen clotted with thrombin > clot lysis time measured

·     Lysis of fibrin plates - standard fibrinogen solution on the Petri dish + CaCl2 + thrombin >clot (solid fibrin plate) >Add euglobulin > plasminogen from fibrin solution converts into plasmin > zone of lysis proportionate to the concentration of tPA in the euglobulin fraction

·     Venous occlusion test - localised venous occlusion stimulates release of tPA from the vessel wall; pre- occlusion and post-occlusion lysis times are measured

·     Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) amidolytic assay - activation of purified plasminogen to plasmin in the presence of fibrinogen fragments which stimulate tPA > plasmin measured using specific chromogenic substrate

·     OR - plasma tPA binds to microtitre-plate Ab > wash > add plasminogen + stimulator of tPA activity

·     measure produced plasmin (chromogenic substrate)

·     tPA released in plasma in active form, binds to PAI-I > inactivation

·     active tPA is only a small fraction of total (antigenic) tPA

·     Plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI) assay - fixed amount of tPA added to undiluted plasma >part of tPA rapidly complexes with PAI-I >plasminogen in plasma is activated by residual tPA>plasmin is measured using plasmin-specific substrate

·     Amount of plasmin directly proportional to the residual tPA activity and inversely proportional to the PAI-I activity

·     Plasmin inhibitor (α2 antiplasmin) amidolytic assay - plasma dilutions incubated with excess plasmin; part of plasmin inhibited by antiplasmins; residual plasmin is measured by a specific chromogenic substrate

·        

*More ROTEM*

A Simplified Treatment-Based Approach to TEG and ROTEM

6/11/2018 Adam Morcom, MD

Case
You receive a 40-year-old trauma patient who is hypotensive after a motor vehicle collision. As your team completes its secondary survey and FAST, you initiate massive transfusion protocol according to the standard 1:1:1 ratio of packed red blood cells to platelets to plasma. But what comes next? Are there additional tools you can use to help guide your resuscitation?

The use of viscoelastic hemostatic assays (VHAs) such as thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) are becoming increasingly common in the ED and trauma bay. While most EM physicians have likely heard of these diagnostic tests before, experience and comfort levels may vary widely when it comes to interpreting and ultimately using these test results to guide blood product transfusions and resuscitation endpoints.

Hades or Pluto?
Much like Greek and Roman mythology are filled with analogues—gods and goddesses who are eerily similar to one another but go by different names depending on which version of the story you read—so can ROTEM, TEG, and other VHAs be thought of as directly analogous to one another. The same properties are being measured, but are labeled with different names from one test to another. The advantage is that once you learn the specifics of a particular platform, it becomes very easy to apply the principles to any of its alternatives.

So what is actually happening in this assay? As blood clots form and strengthen, they exhibit increasing viscosity and elasticity. Physically speaking, both ROTEM and TEG involve the oscillating motion of a cylindrical shaft through a small sample of blood. As the blood forms into a clot, it exerts increasing resistance on the shaft. By measuring this resistance, we are able to track the strength of the forming clot over time. The results of TEG and ROTEM can be displayed as either a two-dimensional graph forming in real-time, or as a numerical list of pre-selected time intervals. Test results are often available in 30 minutes or less.

Figure 1. ROTEM Illustration (from Haemoview Diagnostics)

Both ROTEM and TEG provide a great deal of quantitative data; however, a simple approach to VHA-based treatment begins with focusing on 3 questions about clots:

·        How fast?

·        How strong?

·        For how long?

Figures 2-3 from: Anderson L, Quasim I, Steven M, et al. Interoperator and Intraoperator Variability of Whole Blood Coagulation Assays: A Comparison of Thromboelastography and Rotational Thromboelastometry. J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth. 2014;28(6):1550-1557.

How Fast?
The first question to address is how quickly a new clot begins to form. This stage is represented by the linear portion on the left side of the graph (Figure 2), labeled clotting time (CT) for ROTEM (or specifically ROTEM’s EXTEM test, with re-agents added to isolate the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade), or reaction time (R) for TEG. The time it takes a new clot to begin forming indicates the cumulative functionality of all the higher-level clotting factors within the coagulation cascade, leading up to the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin. Although there may be a great deal of complexity in this portion of the coagulation cascade, for the purposes of emergent bleeding, we can reduce this entire section to a single numerical value. Prolonged CT or R can be treated with fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).

How Strong?
How strong is the new clot once it’s formed? This should be thought of as a two-part question, because there are two major components that give a clot its strength: fibrin and platelets. You may recall that a clot is composed of a platelet plug, reinforced by cross-linked strands of polymerous fibrin chains. A deficiency in either fibrin or platelets will result in a pathologically weak clot. So how can we tell which of these two is deficient? With earlier generations of the technology, we would use a secondary test within either TEG or ROTEM to measure the contribution of fibrin directly, and then we would have to infer the contribution of platelets to clot strength indirectly. More recently, however, the companies that make TEG and ROTEM have released technologies capable of measuring platelet functionality directly, specifically TEG’s PlateletMapping® Assay or ROTEM® Platelet. These newer technologies may or may not be available at a given institution, and so it is still worth learning both the previous and newer methods. (Note that we are focused on platelet functionality, not simply platelet count.)

When assessing clot strength, we are looking at the highest amplitudes within the middle of the graph, namely the maximum clot formation (MCF) in ROTEM, or the maximum amplitude (MA) in TEG. If each of these values is normal, then there is likely no clot strength deficiency. However, if the clot is too weak overall, then we have to assess the two main components separately. Each platform has a devoted test to measure the contribution of fibrin to clot strength: the FIBTEM MCF in ROTEM, or the Functional Fibrinogen (FF) level in TEG. If the fibrin component is deficient, then we should replete it by TRAUMA giving cryoprecipitate. Using the older inference method, if the FIBTEM MCF or FF test is normal, but the overall clot strength (MCF or MA) is deficient, then we can infer that there is a deficiency in platelet functionality, and these should be repleted accordingly.

In some cases, both fibrin and platelets may be deficient. In order to detect this combination using the inference method, whenever you find and treat a deficiency in fibrin, you should run the test a second time. If the fibrin component has been corrected but the overall clot strength remains deficient, this indicates there must be a concurrent platelet deficiency, which should also be treated. Or alternatively, using the newer technologies, we can measure both fibrin and platelets individually and replete whichever is lacking.

For How Long?
Is the patient’s clot as durable as it needs to be, or is the clot breaking down sooner than it should? This is a question of fibrinolysis, represented by the rightward portion of the graph where the amplitude begins to decrease again, corresponding to the process by which plasminogen converts to the active plasmin and begins breaking down fibrin strands. This process occurs normally in healthy patients, however overactive plasmin causes hyperfibrinolysis, which is a treatable form of coagulopathy. To detect hyperfibrinolysis, you may examine the lysis index at 30 minutes (LI30) in ROTEM, or the lysis at 30 or 60 minutes (LY30, LY60) in TEG. If your bleeding patient’s clots are being lysed too quickly, you may treat with tranexamic acid (TXA). (Note that this targeted treatment differs from the guidelines based on the CRASH2 trial, which advises that empiric TXA must be given within the first 3 hours of injury to confer mortality benefit. However, bleeding patients with an identified hyperfibrinolysis represent a different patient population than that of CRASH2, and therefore not subject to the same 3-hour window.)

 

What About Those Other Parameters, Not Discussed Here?
You may notice there are additional parameters listed that have been omitted from this discussion, such as the K value in TEG, the A10 value in ROTEM, and the alpha-angle in both. Each of these parameters occurs after the linear portion of the graph but before the highest amplitude is reached. Therefore, these values will be impacted by a combination of both the higher-level coagulation cascade factors that initiate clot formation and also the components of clot strength, fibrin and platelets.

Although abnormalities in K, A10, or alpha-angle do represent true coagulopathy, we recommend beginning with a simplified treatment algorithm based only on the “purer” parameters we have chosen to highlight here. It should also be noted that abnormalities in K, A10, or alpha-angle will often be accompanied by abnormalities in our highlighted parameters, and so treatment will still be indicated by our algorithm.

What About Patients Taking NOACs?
Novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs) such as rivaroxaban, apixaban, and dabigatran are being used with increasing frequency. Typically these agents target either Factor Xa (in the case of rivaroxaban and apixaban) or thrombin (in the case of dabigatran) within the coagulation cascade. While TEG and ROTEM will accurately identify coagulopathies caused by NOACs, it must be noted that the treatments recommended in our algorithms are likely to be much less effective in countering such coagulopathies, as is regrettably the case with NOACs in general.

A careful history must be taken in order to identify patients taking dabigatran, which has a targeted reversal agent, idarucizumab. Currently there are no targeted reversal agents available for Factor Xa-inhibiting drugs.

When to Use TEG or ROTEM?
In the ED setting, TEG and ROTEM have been studied primarily in the setting of trauma. However, these tests have also been studied to a lesser degree in patients with post-partum hemorrhage, GI bleeding, severe epistaxis, and in selected perioperative patients. In general, ED physicians should consider using TEG or ROTEM in any patient with a serious or life-threatening bleed in order to identify coagulopathies that may be corrected.

In the setting of trauma, studies have shown that both ROTEM- and TEG-guided treatment algorithms result in non-inferior patient outcomes and result in decreased overall usage of blood products compared to empiric massive transfusion protocols.

TEG, ROTEM, and other VHAs are powerful tools that can guide your transfusion of blood products in real-time. Hopefully the simplified algorithms listed here will help you make use of this valuable information.
