ROTEM: The Basic 5 Assays

The ROTEM assay measures the strength of an induced clot (measured in amplitude) as time passes on the x-axis (figure 1). The shape of the curve at various standardized endpoints helps delineate parameters of a given curve that we will talk about later on.

Figure 1. Graphic representation of ROTEM parameters on a ROTEM curve. 2 standardized time reference points are at 10 and 30 minutes for multiple parameters.

ROTEM has 5 different component assays: EXTEM, INTEM, FIBTEM, APTEM,and HEPTEM. A provider needs to specify which assays to run, mostly because not all assays are applicable to each patient situation. Here is the breakdown of each assay:  

  • EXTEM: Analogous to a protime. This tests the extrinsic pathway. 
  • INTEM: Analogous to the APTT. Phospholipid and ellagic acid are added to the initial blood sample, testing the intrinsic pathway.
  • FIBTEM: Platelet inhibitor (cytochalasin D) eliminates platelets’ contribution to clot strength and formation. This test primarily evaluates fibrinogen’s contribution to clot strength.
  • APTEM: The same test and activators as EXTEM with the addition of aprotinin to inhibit fibrinolysis. Stronger clots with higher amplitude, when compared to EXTEM, suggest hyperfibrinolysis in the patient. 
  • HEPTEM: The same test and activators as INTEM with the addition of heparinase. The point is to diagnose underlying coagulopathy that is NOT due to heparin. Order this test if your patient is heparinized (eg. ECLS). In the absence of a heparin infusion, HEPTEM and INTEM will look identical.

Given the assays’ nature, the 2 most useful assays in the ICU or in the resuscitation bay tend to be the EXTEM and the FIBTEM. It is also possible to order ECATEM, which is mainly used in the presence of direct thrombin inhibitors. Given the supplemental nature of HEPTEM and ECATEM and the special circumstances they need to be relevant, we won’t talk about them too much.

Table 1. Summary table of ROTEM components

A standard ROTEM output for a patient not on heparin would classically produce 4 graphs (EXTEM, INTEM, FIBTEM, and APTEM) and relevant parameters for each curve. While the next section deals with those parameters, figure 2 is what those graphs look like.

Figure 2. A normal/control 4-curve output for a ROTEM analysis that includes EXTEM, INTEM, FIBTEM, and APTEM. Notice that both EXTEM and INTEM both normally look like “brandy-sniffing” glasses, that the FIBTEM looks like a narrow champagne flute, and the APTEM resembles a little more of a “chalice” shape.

ROTEM: Basic parameters

The more a person utilizes ROTEM, the sooner they develop an eye for what pathologies “look like” in the data’s graphic representation (similar to reading EKGs). However, it’s important to recognize that ROTEM curves will come with parameters that also help inform decision-making. The basic parameters derive from values on the graphical outputs (see Fig 1), but their actual definitions are as follows:

  • Clot Time (CT): The amount of time it takes for any clot to form. As the clot builds, it will exert a resistive force on the pin spinning in the sample of blood. This often will be quite prolonged in heparin, warfarin, or in patients not able to make factors II, VII, IX, and X.
  • Clot Formation Time (CFT): The amount of time it takes for the amplitude to reach 20 mm. A prolonged CFT suggests impaired or slow clot propagation, often a PLT issue or low fibrinogen.
  • ɑ-angle (ɑ): The angle tangent to the clotting curve at the 2 mm amplitude point. Larger angles indicate more rapid clotting.
  • Amplitude at 10 minutes (A10): The amplitude/ strength of the curve at 10 minutes + CT
  • Maximum Clot Formation (MFT): The maximum strength the clot can produce.
  • Lysis Index (LY30): The amount of clot lysis that has occurred at 30 minutes. Usually this is expressed as a percentage relative to MCF (i.e. LY30 = MCF-A30 min/ MCF).  
  • Maximum Lysis: The amount of clot lysis that occurs for the entire curve (sometimes out to 60 minutes). This is expressed as a percent relative to MCF.

Developing a ROTEM Strategy

ROTEM will only guide management if a resuscitation leader can implement the assay’s data into an actionable strategy in a systematic or strategic way. There are multiple strategies articulated in the available literature cited here and in the Further Reading section.To date, there is no “one” strategy that has been proven most efficacious. Figure 2 and table 2 may help outline ways to both recognize and transfuse based on ROTEM outputs. We have also included some de-identified (but real) patient cases to cement a patient-centered approach to ROTEM.

Figure 2: Some of the common pathologic patterns seen in ROTEM

Table 2. Common ROTEM parameters with treatment implications. Abbreviations: PLT (platelets), Coag (plasma coagulation factors), Cryo (cryoprecipitate), FFP (fresh frozen plasma), TXA (tranexamic acid). *Normal values may differ depending on a center. Always use your lab’s normal reference values. † You may need to review one parameter’s results in the context of another/ different ROTEM assay to understand its meaning fully.

Figure 3: The informal “10-40-80” rule adopted by some centers (commonly practiced in cardiothoracic ORs) can help mnemonic fall back on in the appropriate setting. See Dr. Tanaka’s lecture from the University of Maryland Critical Care Project for a deeper dive.

Patient Examples

Case 1:

A 60-year-old male presented with severe COVID-19 ARDS and was placed on VV-ECMO support. Several days into his course, a dialysis catheter was placed in the left femoral vein to help with volume overload. However, the site began to bleed profusely despite multiple pressure dressings and topical treatment of thrombin. A heparin assay was 0.4 IU/mL. Platelets, Hgb, Fibrinogen, and INR, were normal, though a PTT was elevated to 70.

Figure 5. ROTEM analysis for a patient on VV-ECMO who is heparinized and bleeding

ROTEM explanation: 

The figure classically reflects the effects of heparin but no other underlying coagulopathies. The A10FIBTEM is >10, suggesting no need for Cryo, and the A10EXTEM is >40, arguing against PLT dysfunction. CTEXTEM is only mildly elevated over the quoted standard, but the CTINTEM  is massively elevated at 305. This could indicate a need for aPCC or FFP; however, it could also mean the heparin effect. Luckily, the team sent a HEPTEM, a CT of 206 (normal HEPTEM CT is 100-240). This is a classic ROTEM for a person doing well on ECMO but whose bleeding is primarily due to heparinization. 

Case Resolution: Given the patient was on a heparin bonded circuit, heparin infusion was held. The bandage was taken down, and a purse-string suture was placed along with topical TXA and lidocaine with epinephrine subcutaneously. The heparin infusion resumed 16 hours later with no further bleeding episodes. 

Case 2:

 A 65-year-old patient suffering from septic shock in the setting of Acute on Chronic Liver Failure is on vasopressor support as well as invasive mechanical ventilation and CVVHD. Overnight the nurses report that he began bleeding from multiple IV sites and had coffee ground material sucked up from his OGT. His PLTs are at 31,000 (stable for the last week), his Hgb is 8.0, his INR is 3.2, his fibrinogen is 41 mg/dL, and his D-dimer is 10,270.

Figure 6. ROTEM analysis for a patient with ACLF and bleeding from vascular sites.

ROTEM Explanation:

Here we only have 3 of the five possible assays, which is fine since it’s unlikely HEPTEM or APTEM will be of much use here. The A10FIBTEM is <10, which indicates depleted fibrinogen reserves. The A10EXTEM is <40, suggesting either platelet dysfunction or very low platelet levels responsible for weak clots. CTEXTEM is significantly prolonged, but not CTINTEM, meaning that this may be due in part to low levels of clotting factors rather than this being a heparin effect. The MCF is extremely low, suggesting poor clot stability. In both the EXTEM and INTEM, no narrowing of the curve after MCF is seen, arguing against hyperfibrinolysis. 

Case Resolution: The patient underwent multiple units of cryoprecipitate transfusion, but because of his advanced portal hypertension, FFP was held in reserve but not given. After fibrinogen was related, all bleeding episodes stopped. The team felt reassured that DIC was unlikely.

The Debrief

  • ROTEM is a viscoelastic assay that may be a helpful adjunct to caring for patients in specific circumstances during their resuscitation or ICU course. 

1.    Consider using ROTEM in the following scenarios:

o   Large scale blood resuscitation (MTP activation)

o   Unexplained bleeding episodes

o   Pre, peri, and post-operative and courses for liver and cardiothoracic surgery cases

2.    It is essentially the only lab test that objectively demonstrates fibrinolysis. In cases of suspected DIC or fibrinolytic crisis, it may help clinch the diagnosis.

3.    Develop a familiarity with waveform shapes and parameter metrics and a systematic approach to how you may want to transfuse (and your transfusion targets).

Anticoagulants and DOAC

 

 

DOAC’s effect on routine coagulation assays

·       PT/INR and APTT will be elevated in majority of patients on a DOAC but NON LINEAR dose response

·       Up to 25% of patients on a DOAC will have no increase in PT or APTT (outside of the reference range)

·       There is a differential effect on PT between rivaroxaban and apixaban. PT is often normal on apixaban.

·       PT/INR and APTT CANNOT be used to determine degree of anticoagulation but may help “qualitatively”

 

Quantitative DOAC levels

·       Dabigatran – the Hemoclot assay is based on the thrombin time and calibrated to dabigatran concentration

·       Riva, apix and edo – anti-Xa assays calibrated to the specific drug concentration

Hemophilia and acquired hemophilia drugs

 

Drug

Mechanism of Action (MOA)

Indications

Contraindications

Dosing

rFVIIa
(Recombinant Factor VIIa, e.g., NovoSeven)

Binds tissue factor to activate the extrinsic coagulation pathway, promoting thrombin generation.

- Treatment of bleeding episodes in hemophilia A/B with inhibitors.
- Prevention of surgical bleeding.

- Hypersensitivity.
- Thrombotic disorders (e.g., DIC, active thrombosis).

Acute bleeding: 90–120 mcg/kg IV every 2–3 hours until hemostasis.
Surgery: 90 mcg/kg preoperatively, repeated as needed.

rpFVIII
(Recombinant Porcine FVIII, e.g., Obizur)

Replaces human FVIII in patients with inhibitors by using porcine FVIII to bypass antibodies.

- Bleeding episodes in acquired hemophilia A (anti-human FVIII inhibitors).

- Hypersensitivity to porcine proteins.

Initial dose: 200 IU/kg IV.
Adjustment: Based on FVIII levels and clinical response (target FVIII: 50–100%).

Emicizumab
(e.g., Hemlibra)

Bispecific antibody mimicking FVIII function by bridging FIXa and FX to restore coagulation.

- Prophylaxis in hemophilia A (with or without inhibitors) to reduce bleeding.

- Hypersensitivity.
- Avoid concurrent use of aPCC (↑ thrombotic risk).

Loading: 3 mg/kg SC weekly × 4 weeks.
Maintenance: 1.5–6 mg/kg SC weekly, every 2 weeks, or monthly.

 

COVID19 Coagulopathy may be not important

 

Hypercoagulable state

 

●        COVID-19 is associated with a hypercoagulable state associated with acute inflammatory changes and distinct laboratory findings

o   The predominant coagulation abnormalities in patients with COVID-19 suggest a hypercoagulable state and are consistent with uncontrolled clinical observations of an increased risk of venous thromboembolism

o   This state has been termed thrombo inflammation or COVID-19-associated coagulopathy (CAC) by some experts

o   Note: Lab findings are distinct from acute DIC, with the exception of those with very severe disease (i.e. acute DIC is reported in severely ill COVID 19 patients)

●        Screening coags (INR and aPTT)

o   Typically only modest prolongation of the prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)

o   Presence of a lupus anticoagulant (LAC) is common in individuals with prolonged aPTT

●        Fibrinogen is increased

o   In contrast, acute decompensated DIC is associated with low fibrinogen due to consumption of clotting factors

●        D-dimer is increased

o   Very elevated levels of D-dimer have been observed that correlate with illness severity

●        Platelets

o   Mild thrombocytosis or

o   Mild thrombocytopenia

o   A potential role for platelet activation in promoting thrombosis has been postulated, although data are limited

●        TEG findings

o   Reaction time (R) shortened, consistent with increased early thrombin burst

o   Clot formation time (K) shortened, consistent with increased fibrin generation

o   Maximum amplitude (MA) increased, consistent with greater clot strength

o   Clot lysis at 30 minutes (LY30) reduced, consistent with reduced fibrinolysis

●        Other assays

o   Factor VIII activity increased

o   VWF antigen greatly increased consistent with endothelial injury or inflammation

o   Minor changes in natural anticoagulants

▪          Small decreases in antithrombin and free protein S

▪          Small increase in protein C

Pathogenesis

 

●        Pathogenesis of these abnormalities is incompletely understood

o   May be many contributing factors related to the acute inflammatory response to the disease

Virchow's triad

●        Hypercoagulability can be thought of in terms of Virchow's triad

●        All three of the major contributions to clot formation apply to severe COVID-19 infection:

o   Endothelial injury

▪          There is evidence of direct invasion of endothelial cells by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) virus, potentially leading to cell injury

▪          Postulated that endothelial injury, endothelial inflammation and microvascular inflammation play a central role in the pathogenesis of acute respiratory distress syndrome and organ failure in patients with severe COVID-19

o   Stasis

▪          Immobilization can cause stasis of blood flow in all hospitalized and all critically ill patients, regardless of whether they have COVID-19

o   Hypercoagulable state

▪          A number of changes in circulating prothrombotic factors have been reported or proposed in patients with severe COVID-19 including

●        Elevated factor VIII

●        Elevated fibrinogen

●        Circulating prothrombotic microparticles

●        Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)

●        Hyperviscosity

Thrombosis risk

 

●        Risk for VTE = markedly increase

o   Especially in ICU patients

▪          Case series reporting prevalence of 25 to 43 % in ICU patients

▪          Often despite prophylactic-dose anticoagulation

●        Risk of pulmonary microvascular thrombosis = increased

●        Risk for arterial thrombotic events = increased

o   E.g. stroke, myocardial infarction, and limb ischemia

 

Evaluation

Laboratory testing

●        Goal of testing 🡪 to obtain prognostic information that may be used to inform level of care

●        Inpatients

o   All patients admitted to the hospital for COVID-19 should have baseline investigations

▪          CBC with platelet count

●        Screening coags (INR/PT, aPTT)

▪          Fibrinogen

▪          D-dimer

o   Repeat testing is done as clinically indicated by patient condition

●        Outpatients

o   Do not require coagulation testing

 

Imaging

●        Imaging studies are appropriate for suspected VTE

Management

 

●        Management is challenging due to the acuity of the illness and a paucity of high-quality evidence regarding efficacy and safety of different approaches to prevent or treat thromboembolic complications of the disease

●        General approach includes:

o   1 - Thromboprophylaxis

o   2 - Treatment of VTE

o   3 - Supportive treatment for bleeding

Thromboprophylaxis

●        Inpatients

o   All inpatients should receive thromboprophylaxis unless contraindicated

▪          LMWH - preferred

▪          UFH - can be used if LMWH is unavailable or if kidney function is severely impaired

o   Some institutional protocols include more aggressive anticoagulation with intermediate-dose or even therapeutic-dose anticoagulation for thromboprophylaxis

o   Individuals who have not had a VTE are not routinely given thromboprophylaxis after discharge from the hospital

o   A period of thromboprophylaxis following discharge may be appropriate in selected individuals identified with high risk features

●        Outpatients

o   Individuals who do not require hospital admission for COVID-19 are not treated with antithrombotic agents, with rare exceptions.

VTE treatment

●        Therapeutic-dose (full-dose) anticoagulation is appropriate to treat DVT or PE, unless contraindicated

●        This is continued for at least 3 months

Bleeding

●        Less common than thrombosis but can occur

●        If it occurs, treatment is similar to non-COVID-19 patients (i.e. supportive) and may include

o   Transfusions

▪          PRBCs, PLTs, CRYO/Fib concentrate, FP etc.

o   Anticoagulant reversal or discontinuation

o   Specific products for underlying bleeding disorders

Investigational therapies

●        Disease-specific therapies under investigation may impact thrombotic risk, but the effects of these treatments on hemostasis in COVID-19 have not been well documented

Common agents in hemostasis

Vitamin K (enzyme, genotype)

·       Vitamin K is a group of 2-methilo-naphthoquinone derivatives. There are three forms of vitamin K

o   K1 (phytonadione, phylloquinone, phytonactone); the principal dietary (plants) source of vitamin K and its predominant circulating form.

o   K2 (menaquinones), which can be formed by natural bacteria in the intestines; found in chicken egg yolk, butter, cow liver, certain cheeses and fermented soybean;

o   K3 (menadione),the most active synthetic form; fat-soluble vitamin precursor that is converted into menaquinone in the liver.

·       Very little vitamin K is stored in the liver and in the bones (may play a role in bone calcification), only enough to supply the body's needs for a few days.

·       Vitamin K is involved in the carboxylation of glutamate residues in proteins to form gamma-carboxyglutamate residues. These proteins have in common the requirement to be post-translationally modified by carboxylation of glutamic acid residues (forming gamma-carboxyglutamic acid) in order to become biologically active. These proteins include the vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors II (prothrombin), VII (proconvertin), IX (Christmas factor), X (Stuart factor), protein C, protein S, protein Zv and a growth-arrest-specific factor (Gas6). Common genetic variants in the cytochrome P450 (CYP2C9) and vitamin K-epoxide reductase complex (VKORC1) enzymes, in addition to known non-genetic factors, account for ~50% of warfarin dose variability.

·       Warfarin and acetaminophen interaction, possible contributing factor to INR variability; recommendation (level C evidence): re-test INR 3-5 days after the first Tylenol dose if Tylenol was used in >2g/day over 3 days.

 

 

Warfarin

·       Drugs that increase effect – metronidazole, TMP-SMX, acetaminophen

·       Drugs that decrease effect – EtOH, OCP, prednisone, barbiturates

 

 

Ø  Mechanism of action for heparin and warfarin, their reversals as well as all other new anticoagulant drugs

·     Heparin - Proteoglycan from mast cell secretory granules, mixture of glycosaminoglycans from 3KD to 30KD. Binds AT and induces conformational change → accelerates binding to FXa and free thrombin

o   Monitor: aPTT, anti-Xa

·     LMWH - Proteoglycan from mast cell secretory granules, 5KD

o   Binds AT and induces conformational change → accelerates binding to FXa (too short to bind thrombin)

o   Monitor: anti-Xa

·     Warfarin - Vitamin K antagonist, blocks gamma-carboxylation (vitamin K epoxide reductase) and functional activity of vitamin K-dependent proteins (II, VII, IX, X). Can be reversed by vitamin K.

o   Monitor: INR

·     Danaparoid - Low molecular weight heparinoid consisting of heparin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate

o   Inhibits thrombin but inhibits factor Xa more selectively (28:1 vs 3:1 with LMWH)

o   Monitor: anti-Xa

o   Long half-life, renal excretion

·     Fondaparinux - Synthetic pentasaccharide,

o   binds AT as a selective Xa inhibitor

·     Argatroban - Direct inhibitor of thrombin – binds proteolytic site (free and fibrin-bound thrombin)

o   Monitor: PTT

o   Short half-life, liver excretion

·     Hirudin - Polypeptide from leech salivary gland

o   Direct inhibitor of thrombin – bivalently binds proteolytic site and substrate recognition site (free and fibrin-bound thrombin)

o   Monitor: PTT

o   Long half-life, renal excretion, anti-hirudin antibodies in 40%

·     Apixaban (Eliquis)-oral direct FXa inhibitor;

o   12 hours half-life; 25% renal excretion;

o   2.5 mg BID; VTE prophylaxis post-knee of hip surgery; 12-24 h. post-surgery initial dose; hip-32-38 days; knee-10-14 days;

o   ARISTOTLE trial: superior to warfarin in a.fib pts (less bleeding, fewer strokes);

o   Not approved for a.fib by FDA yet;

·     Rivaroxaban - FXa inhibitor;

o   ROCKET trial: rivaroxaban vs warfarin: the rates of intracranial hemorrhage and fatal bleeding were lower with rivaroxaban than with warfarin, but there was no advantage with respect to other major bleeding.

o   Approved by Health Canada for VTE prophylaxis in knee and hip surgery; for stroke prevention in afib pts (January 2012); once daily dose

·     Dabigatran - direct thrombin inhibitor;

o   Re-Ly trial (dabigatran vs warfarin)- non-inferiority study: 150-mg dose of dabigatran administered twice daily, as compared with warfarin, was shown to reduce the rate of stroke, including ischemic or unspecified stroke, with a similar overall rate of bleeding, although the rate of gastrointestinal bleeding was increased. The 110-mg dose administered twice daily was associated with a rate of stroke that was similar to that with warfarin but with a lower rate of major bleeding. Both doses resulted in lower rates of intracranial hemorrhage.

o   Approved in Canada for VTE prophylaxis post knee and hip surgery and for stroke prevention in a.fib; contraindicated for pts with renal failure (CrCl<30), mechanical heart valve, significant bleeding risk;

 

Ø Heparin resistance: causes; treatment

·     Patients need unusually large doses of heparin to achieve therapeutic aPTT (>35,000 units in 24 hours)

·     Causes:

A. Antithrombin (AT) Deficiency

o   Most common cause

o   Heparin requires AT to exert its anticoagulant effect

o   Can be congenital or more often acquired (e.g., in critical illness, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, DIC)

B. Elevated Heparin-Binding Proteins

o   Inflammatory states (e.g., surgery, trauma, sepsis) increase acute phase reactants that bind and neutralize heparin

C. Increased Clearance / Volume of Distribution

o   Seen in obesity, pregnancy, or high-output states

o   Leads to more heparin being needed to reach effective plasma concentration

D. High Factor VIII or Fibrinogen Levels

o   Common in inflammatory states

o   Can shorten aPTT, masking heparin effect despite adequate anticoagulation

E. Laboratory Artifact

o   Reliance on aPTT alone can be misleading in certain settings (e.g., lupus anticoagulant, elevated factor VIII)

·     Treatment:

o   Adjust heparin to anti-factor Xa activity of 0.35 to 0.7 IU/mL

o   No difference in VTE and bleeding than if you use target aPTT of 60 to 80 seconds, but lower doses of heparin required

o   Can give plasma-derived ATIII if AT deficient

 

Ø A patient is receiving LMWH. How would you monitor? Which patients require monitoring?

·     Monitoring generally not necessary, because of predictable weight-based dose response

·     May monitor in renal insufficiency (CrCl < 30), obesity (wt > 150 kg), pregnancy, recurrent DVT already on LMWH

·     Monitor with anti-factor Xa assay at 2-4 hours after administration based on manufacturer dosing guidelines (anti-Xa 0.5 – 1.0 U/mL)

Uncommon agents in hemostasis

 

Aprotinin:

  • Class: antifibrinolytic

·        Aprotinin (bovine protein; Trasylol, previously Bayer and now Nordic Group pharmaceuticals).

·        It inhibits fibrinolysis via action on plasmin and kallikrein .

·        Its action on kallikrein leads to the inhibition of the formation of factor XIIa. As a result, both the intrinsic pathway of coagulation and fibrinolysis are inhibited.

·        Its action on plasmin independently slows fibrinolysis.

·        Not used for treatment since 2008 (increased risk of kidney failure and death); could be added to blood samples of pts on fibrinolytic therapy to inhibit in vitro fibrinolysis.

·        Type 2M vWD involves qualitatively defective VWF with normal multimer structure, leading to decreased platelet adhesion due to mutations affecting the A1 or A3 domains.

·        It presents with a normal multimer pattern, a decreased response to high-dose RIPA, and a decreased VWF/VWFratio. It is the opposite of Type 2B, which shows increased response to low-dose ristocetin and loss of large multimers.

 [QZ3]low dose is sensitive to the presence of abnormalities in VWF or platelet GpIb interactions.

 [QZ4]Type 2B vWD: Shows an increased response to low-dose RIPA but generally normal or mildly reduced high-dose RIPA.

Type 2M vWD: Shows a decreased response to high-dose RIPA due to defective VWF-platelet interactions, despite normal multimeric structure.

Bernard-Soulier Syndrome: Both low- and high-dose RIPA are impaired because the GpIb receptor itself is defective.
